title: How Lettering and Translation Choices Change a Scene
question: How do translation and lettering choices change how a manga scene reads?
summary: Japanese carries social information in speech that English lacks a direct mechanism for — honorifics, formality levels, pronoun choice. Every translation has to decide whether to preserve, replace or discard that layer, and the decision materially changes characterisation. 204 in the letters, reducing to 6.
body:
6Reduced, this question gives 6. It sits on The Care with the rest of an obligation.

What Japanese encodes that English does not

Japanese speech carries continuous social information English handles through tone or not at all:

  • Honorifics attached to names mark relative status, familiarity and affection.
  • Formality levels change verb forms entirely, so the same sentence can be polite, neutral or blunt.
  • Pronoun choice is expressive. There are numerous first-person pronouns carrying gender, age, formality and self-presentation.

None of this is decoration. A character switching from a formal to a casual register mid-conversation is a plot event. If the translation renders both identically, the event vanishes.

The honorifics argument

The long-running dispute is whether to keep honorifics in English text.

Keeping them preserves relationships exactly, and the moment a character drops one is legible. The cost is that English prose reads as partly untranslated, and new readers meet unexplained vocabulary immediately.

Dropping them produces cleaner English but forces the translator to smuggle the same information back through word choice and address. Skilled translators manage this; the loss is that it becomes diffuse rather than precise.

Neither approach is correct. This is a philosophy difference, not a quality difference, though it is frequently argued as though it were.

Lettering is characterisation

Lettering is often assumed to be typesetting. It is closer to performance.

Font choice separates narration from dialogue from thought. Bubble shape carries tone — jagged for shouting, dashed or cloudy for whispers and interior thought. Text size within a bubble encodes volume, and a single enlarged word does what italics do in prose but louder. A character whose dialogue is consistently set in a distinct font is being characterised typographically.

Bad lettering is invisible in the wrong way: uniform bubbles and one font flatten a cast into a single voice.

The vertical-to-horizontal problem

Japanese text runs vertically, so bubbles are drawn tall and narrow. English runs horizontally and needs width. Every English release fits horizontal text into vertical containers.

This is why English manga bubbles sometimes look sparse or awkwardly broken across lines, and why translators work to a character count as well as a meaning. A more accurate rendering that does not fit is not usable, so concision routinely wins over precision.

What this means for reading

If a translation feels stiff, the cause is often geometric rather than incompetent. And if two versions of the same series read very differently, they are usually not disagreeing about meaning — they are making different decisions about how much of the Japanese social layer to carry across.

faq.answer: It is a philosophy difference. Keeping them preserves relative status and familiarity precisely, so a character dropping one registers as an event. Removing them produces cleaner English but requires the translator to convey the same information diffusely through word choice. Neither approach is inherently more accurate.

faq.question: What does Japanese encode that English does not?
faq.answer: Honorifics marking status and familiarity, formality levels that change verb forms entirely, and expressive pronoun choice carrying gender, age and self-presentation. A character shifting register mid-conversation is a plot event in Japanese. If a translation renders both registers identically, that event disappears from the scene.

faq.question: Is lettering just typesetting?
faq.answer: No, it is closer to performance. Font choice distinguishes narration, dialogue and thought; bubble shape carries tone, with jagged edges for shouting and cloudy outlines for interior monologue; text size encodes volume. A character given a consistently distinct font is being characterised typographically rather than through dialogue alone.

faq.question: Why do English manga bubbles sometimes look awkward?
faq.answer: Because Japanese runs vertically, so bubbles are drawn tall and narrow, while English runs horizontally and needs width. Every English release fits horizontal text into containers shaped for vertical text. Translators therefore work to character counts as well as meaning, and concision frequently wins over precision.

faq.question: If two translations read differently, is one wrong?
faq.answer: Usually not. They are rarely disagreeing about what the Japanese means. More often they have made different decisions about how much of the social register to carry into English, and how to fit the result into bubbles shaped for vertical text. Both can be defensible renderings of the same line.

title: A Short History of Manga
question: How did manga develop into what it is today?
summary: Modern manga is a postwar phenomenon built on cheap print, magazine serialisation and a small number of enormously influential creators. Claims tracing it to medieval scrolls are popular but historically shaky — the continuous line runs back only about eighty years. Filed under 9, the closing.
body:
9The letters of this question total 99, a 9 — the number of endings, compassion, and the closing of cycles.

The origin story worth treating carefully

You will frequently read that manga descends from twelfth-century picture scrolls, or from Hokusai's sketchbooks, which used the word manga in 1814.

Both claims are real facts arranged into a misleading shape. The scrolls are sequential art and the word does appear in Hokusai, but neither connects by any continuous tradition to what appeared in the 1950s. Most historians treat modern manga as a postwar development shaped far more by imported American comics and film than by medieval Japanese art. The long lineage is a nice story and mostly a retrospective one.

Postwar conditions

The immediate precondition was cheapness. In the impoverished years after 1945, extremely low-cost comics — rented from shops rather than bought, or sold as cheap paperbacks — reached a mass readership. Paper was poor, printing was crude, and volume was everything.

This period established the economics that still govern the medium: high page counts, low unit prices, black and white.

Tezuka and story manga

Osamu Tezuka is conventionally credited with establishing long-form narrative manga, beginning with work in the late 1940s. His significance is genuine, though the popular version overstates it — he did not single-handedly invent the techniques attributed to him, and he was working alongside other innovators.

What is not in dispute is scale of influence. He demonstrated that comics could sustain novel-length stories with serious themes, and a generation of creators trained directly or indirectly in his orbit.

Gekiga and the push toward adult work

By the late 1950s a group of artists wanted a term that distinguished their grittier, more realistic work from comics aimed at children. Gekiga — roughly dramatic pictures — was coined around 1957 for this purpose.

The gekiga movement is the direct ancestor of the seinen category. It established that the medium could handle crime, poverty, violence and political material for adult readers, and its visual influence on later realist manga is enormous.

The magazine era

The weekly anthology magazine consolidated in the late 1950s and 1960s, and it is the single most consequential structure in manga's history. Weekly serialisation with reader-survey feedback created the pacing, the chapter rhythm, the cancellation culture and the volume of output that define the medium.

By the 1980s and into the mid-1990s the largest magazines reached circulation figures that no comics market elsewhere has approached before or since.

Contraction and the digital shift

Magazine circulation has declined substantially since its mid-1990s peak, following the general decline of print. The industry did not shrink correspondingly, because it moved: digital distribution, app-based serialisation, web-first platforms, and an international market that barely existed in 1995.

The current period is defined by that shift. Web serialisation has loosened magazine gatekeeping, colour and vertical-scroll formats are pressing in from Korean webtoons, and overseas revenue now matters to a degree it never used to.

faq.question: Did manga really begin with medieval picture scrolls?
faq.answer: Probably not in any meaningful sense. Twelfth-century scrolls are sequential art and Hokusai did use the word manga in 1814, but neither connects by continuous tradition to what emerged in the 1950s. Most historians treat modern manga as a postwar development shaped more by American comics and film.

faq.question: What was gekiga?
faq.answer: A movement beginning in the late 1950s whose artists wanted a term distinguishing grittier, realistic work from comics for children. The word, coined around 1957, translates roughly as dramatic pictures. Gekiga is the direct ancestor of the seinen category and established that the medium could handle adult subject matter.

faq.question: Why were postwar conditions important?
faq.answer: Because they established the economics that still govern manga. In the impoverished years after 1945, extremely cheap comics — often rented rather than bought — reached mass readership on poor paper with crude printing. High page counts, low prices and black-and-white printing all descend from that period.

faq.question: What made the weekly magazine so consequential?
faq.answer: It is arguably the single most important structure in manga's history. Weekly serialisation combined with reader-survey feedback produced the chapter rhythm, the pacing conventions, the cancellation culture and the sheer volume of output that characterise the medium. Nearly every distinctive trait traces back to it.

faq.question: Is the manga industry shrinking?
faq.answer: Magazine circulation has declined substantially since its mid-1990s peak, in line with print generally, but the industry did not contract correspondingly. It shifted to digital distribution, app-based and web-first serialisation, and an international market that barely existed in 1995 and now matters considerably.

title: Osamu Tezuka and the Invention of Modern Manga
question: Why is Osamu Tezuka called the god of manga?
summary: Tezuka demonstrated that comics could sustain long, serious narrative, produced an enormous body of work across every register, and trained or influenced most of the generation that followed. The popular claim that he personally invented manga's visual language is an overstatement of a real achievement. The question reduces to 3 — the telling.
body:
3Filed under 3. The Telling takes an act of telling, and this explainer is performs one.

Who he was

Osamu Tezuka (1928–1989) was a manga artist and animator whose career spanned the entire formative period of the modern medium. He is routinely called the god of manga, and his output was genuinely enormous — tens of thousands of pages across four decades.

He trained as a doctor and qualified, which surfaces repeatedly in his work's preoccupation with bodies, medicine and mortality.

What he actually established

His central contribution was demonstrating that comics could carry long-form serious narrative. Before his generation, the dominant model was short humorous strips. His work showed that a comic could run for hundreds or thousands of pages, develop characters over time, and address death, war, prejudice and ethics without ceasing to be popular entertainment.

He also worked across a remarkable range — children's adventure, science fiction, medical drama, historical epic, religious biography and explicitly adult material — which made the case that the medium had no inherent subject limits.

The cinematic technique claim, examined

The standard account credits Tezuka with importing film language into comics: varied camera angles, panels functioning as shots, sequences that cut and pan.

This is broadly true and frequently overstated. He did use such techniques prominently and popularised them, but he was not the sole originator, comparable experiments were happening elsewhere, and scholars have pushed back on the tidier versions of the story. The honest framing is that he was the most visible and influential practitioner of an approach that was emerging more broadly.

The animation side

Tezuka founded an animation studio and drove the early television anime industry. This part of his legacy is genuinely double-edged.

He established that a weekly animated series was possible on a small budget, which built the industry. He also did so by accepting extremely low licensing fees and pioneering severe cost-saving techniques. The resulting expectation of cheap animation labour is frequently cited as a root of the anime industry's persistent pay problems, and this criticism was made during his lifetime.

Why his influence compounds

Influence in manga is unusually traceable because of the assistant system. Artists who worked under or near Tezuka went on to their own serialisations, and their assistants did the same. A very large share of the medium's subsequent development descends through that chain.

Reading him now

His work has aged unevenly. The formal ambition and structural boldness hold up; some of the humour, and some depictions in older work, reflect their period in ways modern readers find uncomfortable. His later, darker work is generally the better entry point for adult readers than the children's material he is most famous for.

faq.answer: Principally, the demonstration that comics could sustain long-form serious narrative rather than short humorous strips. He showed a comic could run thousands of pages, develop characters over time and handle death, war and ethics while remaining popular. He also worked across an unusually wide range of genres and registers.

faq.answer: He popularised it, but the claim that he invented it is an overstatement. He used varied angles and film-like sequencing prominently and influentially, though comparable experiments were happening elsewhere and scholars have challenged the tidier versions of this account. He was the most visible practitioner of an emerging approach.

But he did so by accepting very low licensing fees and pioneering severe cost-cutting, and the resulting expectation of cheap animation labour is frequently blamed for the industry's enduring pay problems.

faq.answer: Largely because of the assistant system, which makes influence unusually traceable in manga. A substantial share of the medium's later development descends through that chain of direct working relationships.

title: How Weekly Shonen Jump Shaped What Manga Looks Like
question: Why has Weekly Shonen Jump been so influential?
summary: Jump's reader-survey system converts weekly popularity directly into editorial decisions, including rapid cancellation. Because it became the most commercially successful magazine, that model propagated outward, and much of what people think of as manga's natural form is really Jump's method. Filed under 8, the ledger.
body:
8Reduced, this question gives 8. It sits on The Ledger with the rest of a reckoning.

The magazine

Weekly Shonen Jump has been published by Shueisha since 1968. It runs roughly twenty series at once, each contributing a chapter of about nineteen pages every week, sold cheaply on poor paper.

It is not the only major shonen magazine — competitors launched earlier — but it became the most commercially dominant, and dominance made its methods into defaults.

The survey system

Jump's defining mechanism is the reader survey. Readers rank the series they liked, and results feed directly into editorial decisions with unusual speed.

The consequences are visible on the page:

  • Front-loaded appeal. A new series must establish its hook almost immediately, because early rankings determine survival.
  • Chapter-level hooks. Every instalment needs a reason to return, producing the cliffhanger rhythm characteristic of the format.
  • Rapid cancellation. Poorly ranked series end fast, frequently around chapter twenty, often forcing an author to compress a planned long story into a handful of rushed chapters.
  • Extension of hits. The reverse pressure is equally real. A commercially successful series may be kept running well past its natural ending, which is a recognised cause of quality decline in long-running titles.

Friendship, effort, victory

Jump's frequently cited editorial themes are usually presented as the formula for battle shonen. The framing is real but reductive — the magazine's actual catalogue includes comedy, sports, horror, cooking and psychological thrillers that fit the slogan poorly or not at all.

What the themes do capture accurately is a preference for protagonists defined by persistence rather than talent, which does recur across a great deal of its output.

Why its influence exceeded its pages

Commercial success made Jump the reference point. Rival magazines adopted comparable feedback mechanisms; creators internalised its pacing expectations; and international readers, encountering Jump titles first, came to treat its conventions as manga's conventions.

Much of what a Western reader considers typical of manga — escalating tournaments, power systems, weekly cliffhangers, enormous page counts — is more accurately typical of Jump.

The costs

The model is hard on creators. Constant ranking pressure, weekly deadlines and the threat of abrupt cancellation are a recognised contributor to the health problems and hiatuses common among serialised artists. It optimises effectively for reader engagement, and the price is paid by the people producing the pages.

Its current position

Print circulation has fallen a long way from its mid-1990s peak, but the magazine adapted through digital subscription and official same-week English release, and its major series remain the most commercially significant in the medium.

title: The 1990s Manga Boom and Its Aftermath
question: What happened during the 1990s manga boom?
summary: The mid-1990s were the commercial peak of print manga, with magazine circulation reaching levels never matched since. The decline that followed was a print decline rather than an industry one, and it pushed manga toward digital distribution and international markets. The question reduces to 4 — the structure.
body:
4Filed under 4. The Structure takes a structure, and this explainer is frames one.

The peak

Manga magazine circulation reached its high point in the mid-1990s. The largest weeklies achieved figures in the millions per issue — numbers no comics market anywhere has approached before or since, and which are difficult to convey to readers who only know the current landscape.

This was a genuinely mass medium in the way broadcast television was: a substantial fraction of a country reading the same chapters in the same week.

What drove it

A cluster of extraordinarily popular series ran simultaneously, several of which became internationally recognised. Anime adaptations amplified their reach and fed readers back to the magazines. Home video and merchandising built revenue streams beyond print.

Crucially, the audience that grew up with manga in the 1970s and 1980s had not stopped reading, so the market was serving children and adults at once rather than replacing one with the other.

The decline

Circulation has fallen substantially and continuously since. The causes are mostly not specific to manga: print media declined broadly, competing entertainment multiplied, and Japan's demographics shifted with a shrinking younger population.

It is important to be precise about what fell. Magazine circulation collapsed. Total manga readership and revenue did not follow it down nearly as steeply, because reading moved rather than stopped.

Where it moved

  • Collected volumes became relatively more important than magazines, which increasingly function as a serialisation venue and marketing device rather than a profit centre in themselves.
  • Digital distribution grew from nothing to a very large share of the market, and now exceeds print for many publishers.
  • App-based and web-first serialisation loosened magazine gatekeeping, letting series find audiences without a magazine slot.
  • International markets grew from marginal to strategically significant, which changed which series get licensed and how quickly.

The aftermath in what gets made

These shifts show up in the work. Web-first serialisation removed some of the survey pressure that shaped magazine manga, allowing series with slower openings or narrower appeal to survive. Digital publication made colour and variable chapter lengths practical. Competition from Korean vertical-scroll webtoons has pushed some publishers toward that format.

The result is a more fragmented medium than the 1990s one. There is no longer a single magazine whose rankings function as a proxy for national taste, which is a loss of coherence and a gain in range.

faq.answer: Magazine circulation collapsed, but total readership and revenue did not fall nearly as steeply. Reading moved rather than stopped — toward collected volumes, digital distribution, app-based serialisation and international markets. The decline was principally a print decline rather than an industry-wide contraction.

faq.answer: Mostly factors not specific to manga: the broad decline of print media, a proliferation of competing entertainment options, and Japan's demographic shift toward a smaller younger population. Magazines also became less central as collected volumes and digital sales grew relatively more important to publishers.

faq.question: How did the shift change what gets published?
faq.answer: Web-first serialisation removed some survey pressure, letting series with slower openings or narrower appeal survive. The overall effect is a wider range of work than the magazine era supported.

faq.answer: Increasingly they function as a serialisation venue and marketing device rather than a profit centre. The commercial weight has shifted to collected volumes, digital sales and adaptation rights. Magazines still confer legitimacy and editorial support, but they no longer dominate the economics the way they did in the 1990s.

title: How Manga Reached English-Language Readers
question: How did manga become available in English?
summary: English manga went through three phases: scattered, heavily localised releases in the late 1980s and 1990s, a bookstore-driven boom in the 2000s built on cheap unflipped volumes, and a collapse and digital rebuild that produced today's same-week official releases. Filed under 5, the turn.
body:
5The letters of this question total 176, a 5 — the number of freedom, disruption, and restless movement.

Phase one: scattered and heavily altered

The first sustained English manga releases arrived in the late 1980s. They were few, expensive, and treated as an unusual import.

Crucially, they were heavily localised. Artwork was mirrored so it read left to right. Sound effects were replaced. Names were sometimes changed, and content was edited. Titles were often issued as monthly floppy comics on the American model rather than as volumes, which suited neither the material nor its readers.

This period established a small dedicated audience but no mass market.

Phase two: the bookstore boom

The 2000s changed the picture, and the mechanism was as much retail as editorial. Publishers moved to cheap paperback volumes shelved in general bookstores rather than comic shops, at a price point close to a mass-market novel.

Two decisions mattered enormously. Volumes rather than floppies matched how manga is actually read. And publishers stopped flipping the artwork, marketing the unflipped format as authentic — which turned out to be something readers preferred rather than tolerated.

The result was rapid growth, a much younger and substantially female readership than American comics had, and shelf space in every large bookstore.

Phase three: contraction

The boom overextended. Publishers licensed aggressively, the bookstore chains that carried the volumes ran into their own trouble, and the 2008 financial crisis compounded it. A major manga publisher collapsed in 2011, stranding numerous series mid-release.

This is why a certain generation of series exists in English as an incomplete run of volumes with no prospect of completion — the rights lapsed with a publisher that no longer exists.

Phase four: the digital rebuild

Recovery came through digital. Costs of bringing over a marginal title fell dramatically without print runs and warehousing, which widened the licensed catalogue enormously. Subscription services made sampling nearly free.

The decisive change was simulpub: official English chapters released the same week as Japan. This removed the one genuine advantage unofficial fan translations had held for two decades.

Where that leaves things

The English catalogue is far larger, far cheaper to access and far faster than at any earlier point. Real gaps remain — older titles, commercially marginal categories, and josei in particular are underrepresented — but the situation that produced scanlation in the first place has substantially, if not entirely, closed.

faq.question: Why was early English manga flipped and edited?
faq.answer: Publishers assumed readers would not accept right-to-left reading, so artwork was mirrored to read left to right. Sound effects were replaced, names sometimes changed and content edited. The approach created reversed handedness and backwards signage, and it was largely abandoned once unflipped releases proved commercially successful.

faq.question: What caused the 2000s manga boom in English?
faq.answer: Largely a retail and format shift. Publishers moved to cheap paperback volumes shelved in general bookstores rather than comic shops, priced near a mass-market novel. Volumes matched how manga is actually read, and keeping the artwork unflipped turned out to be something readers preferred rather than merely tolerated.

faq.question: Why are some English manga series incomplete?
faq.answer: Many were stranded when publishers collapsed, particularly around 2011 after the boom overextended and bookstore chains struggled. Rights lapsed with companies that no longer exist, leaving series with an incomplete run of volumes, out of print and often not digitised, unless another publisher later reacquires them.

faq.question: How did digital change availability?
faq.answer: It dramatically lowered the cost of bringing over a marginal title, since there are no print runs or warehousing, which widened the licensed catalogue considerably. Subscription services also made sampling nearly free, and simulpub delivered official English chapters the same week as Japan for major series.

faq.question: Are there still gaps in what is available?
faq.answer: Yes. Older titles are underrepresented because the market for decades-old manga is small, commercially marginal categories often go unlicensed, and josei in particular is thin in English relative to its output in Japan. The gaps are much narrower than a decade ago but have not closed entirely.

title: How a Manga Gets Serialized
question: How does a manga go from an idea to a published series?
summary: The usual route runs through a one-shot or a submitted storyboard, an assigned editor, an editorial board decision, and then a survey-driven probation period in which most new series are cancelled within a year. 107 in the letters, reducing to 8.
body:
8Reduced, this question gives 8. It sits on The Ledger with the rest of a reckoning.

Getting in the door

There are a few standard routes to a magazine's attention. Publishers run competitions for new creators, with winning entries printed and the artist assigned an editor. Artists submit work directly to editorial departments, which is common and slow. And a great many creators arrive having worked as an assistant on an existing series, which supplies both craft experience and a professional contact.

The web has added a genuine fourth route: building a readership on a personal or platform account until an editor approaches you. This has become substantially more common.

The one-shot as audition

The conventional next step is a one-shot — a complete self-contained story of perhaps 30 to 60 pages printed in the magazine. It demonstrates that a creator can carry a whole narrative, not just draw well.

Reader surveys on the one-shot inform whether a serialisation follows. Frequently the premise is substantially reworked between the one-shot and the series that grows out of it, usually at editorial direction.

Name: the storyboard stage

Before any finished page exists, a creator produces a name — a rough storyboard laying out panels, dialogue and page composition in crude sketch form.

This is where the editor's influence concentrates. Names go back and forth, sometimes repeatedly, and an editor may reject many before approving one. Because the name fixes pacing and layout, this stage determines most of what the finished chapter will be. It is the least visible and most consequential part of the process.

The serialisation meeting

A magazine's editorial board decides which proposals get slots. Slots are scarce and contested — an approved series displaces something else. Proposals are judged on the name, the one-shot's survey performance, and the editor's advocacy.

Probation by survey

Approval is not security. New series enter a probation period governed by reader rankings from the earliest chapters.

Most do not survive. Cancellation within the first year is the normal outcome rather than the exception, and it often arrives with only a few chapters' notice, forcing a creator to compress a planned long story into a rushed conclusion.

This is why so many manga have abrupt endings, and why new series front-load their hooks so aggressively.

If it survives

A successful series settles into a weekly or monthly production cycle: name, approval, layout, drawing, assistants applying backgrounds and tone, delivery, repeat. Chapters accumulate until roughly nine or ten can be collected into a volume, which is where the money actually is.

Success creates its own pressure. A commercially strong series may be extended past its intended ending, which is a recognised cause of decline in long-running titles — the mirror image of the cancellation problem.

title: What a Manga Editor Actually Does
question: What does a manga editor do?
summary: A manga editor is closer to a collaborator and producer than to a proofreader. They shape premises before serialisation, approve storyboards chapter by chapter, enforce deadlines, and transmit commercial pressure from the magazine to the creator. The question reduces to 1 — the opening.
body:
1A 1 by its question: leader & pioneer, and therefore the opening.

Not a copy editor

Readers from other publishing traditions consistently underestimate this role. A manga editor is assigned to a creator and functions as first reader, creative collaborator, deadline enforcer, and the channel between the artist and the magazine's editorial board.

The relationship is close and often long-running. Creators routinely name a specific editor as decisive to their career, and editors move between series carrying reputations of their own.

Where the influence actually lands

The concentrated point of intervention is the name, the rough storyboard produced before any finished art. Editors review names chapter by chapter and can reject them, and revisions are normal rather than exceptional.

Because the storyboard fixes pacing, panel layout and dialogue, an editor shaping the name is shaping the chapter itself — before a single finished page exists. It is the least visible part of the process and the most consequential.

Before a series even starts

Editors work with creators on the premise, often through several complete rewrites. A number of well-known series exist in their published form because an editor rejected earlier versions and pushed for something different.

They also advocate internally. Getting a serialisation slot means persuading the editorial board, and an editor's willingness to champion a proposal materially affects whether it runs.

Transmitting commercial pressure

This is the part with a genuine edge to it. Editors relay reader survey data, and doing so carries implicit instruction. Rankings dropping means something must change.

They also transmit the two structural pressures of the magazine model: ending a series that is underperforming, and extending one that is succeeding past the point the author intended. Neither is comfortable, and both come through the editor.

Deadline management

The prosaic function is keeping weekly pages arriving. In practice this means managing an exhausted person under sustained physical strain — arranging schedules, sometimes negotiating a break, sometimes pushing when a break is what is needed.

How well editors handle this varies enormously, and accounts from creators range from deep gratitude to serious criticism.

Where you can see it

Author sidebars in collected volumes are one of the few consistent public windows into these relationships, and creators are often candid there about arguments with editors and which decisions were not theirs.

title: Why Manga Series Go on Hiatus
question: Why do manga series go on hiatus?
summary: Most hiatuses are caused by the creator's health, because weekly serialisation is physically punishing and the work is concentrated in one person. Since manga is closely identified with a single author, there is rarely any mechanism for a series to continue without them. Read from the ledger, as an 8.
body:
8Filed under 8. The Ledger takes a reckoning, and this explainer is commands one.

The structural cause

A weekly serialised manga requires roughly nineteen finished pages every week, indefinitely, from a creator who is usually writing and drawing both. Assistants handle backgrounds and tone, but the storyboard, the layout, the figures and the direction are one person's work.

Sustained over years, this is a physically damaging schedule, and the resulting health problems are the single most common cause of hiatus.

What actually goes wrong

  • Repetitive strain injuries to hands, wrists, shoulders and back — the direct consequence of drawing at that volume.
  • Exhaustion and stress-related illness, from schedules that routinely eliminate normal sleep.
  • Eyesight problems, from years of close detailed work.
  • Surgery and recovery, which for a manual profession means a hard stop rather than reduced output.

These are not unusual outcomes. They are common enough to be treated within the industry as an expected hazard.

The other reasons

Not every hiatus is medical. Creators pause for research, particularly on historical or technical series. Some stop to plan a story's next phase properly, having reached a point where weekly improvisation will not carry it. Bereavement and family circumstances account for others. Occasionally a break follows a dispute with a publisher.

Short versus indefinite

Short scheduled breaks are routine and unremarkable — a skipped week, or a magazine's planned publication gap.

Indefinite hiatus is a different matter. A series stops with no stated return date, and may not come back. Because manga is so closely tied to one creator's hand and voice, there is rarely any mechanism to continue a work without them. Unlike a superhero comic, another artist cannot simply take over.

The result is that some series are left permanently unfinished, occasionally very close to their conclusion.

Why readers should factor it in

Before committing to a long ongoing series, it is worth checking its publication status and recent release pattern. Ongoing means waiting. A history of long gaps means waiting more. Indefinite hiatus may mean never.

This is not a reason to avoid ongoing work, but it is a reason to know what you are starting.

The wider point

Hiatuses are the visible symptom of a production model that extracts a great deal from individuals. Criticism of manga working conditions comes from within the profession as much as outside it, and reader frustration with delays sits awkwardly against the reason the delays exist.

title: How Manga Creators Are Paid
question: How do manga creators make money?
summary: Income comes mainly from a per-page serialisation fee and royalties on collected volumes, with adaptation and merchandising rights mattering for the few big successes. The page fee is often modest, and creators frequently pay their own assistants out of it. The question reduces to 1 — the opening.
body:
1Filed under 1. The Opening takes a first move, and this explainer is declares one.

The page rate

Serialised creators are paid a fee per published page. This is the reliable, predictable component of income, and for most working manga artists it is the bulk of what they earn.

Rates vary by magazine and by the creator's standing, and are generally not published. The consistent theme in accounts from creators is that the page rate alone is a modest living at best, and thin for anyone at the start of a career.

Assistants come out of it

This is the detail that most changes the picture. In many arrangements, a creator pays their assistants from their own page fee rather than the publisher employing them directly.

Since weekly serialisation is not physically possible without assistants, this is not an optional expense. A creator's headline income therefore substantially overstates what they keep, and a series that looks successful can be close to break-even once studio costs are met.

Volume royalties

The real money is in collected volumes. Creators receive a royalty on each tankobon sold, and for a series with a substantial readership this dwarfs the page rate.

This is why volume sales figures matter so much in industry discussion, and why cancellation is so consequential: a series ended before it accumulates volumes never reaches the part of the model where creators actually earn.

It also explains the sharp inequality in outcomes. A handful of enormous successes generate significant wealth; the large majority of serialised creators do not approach that.

Adaptation and merchandising

Anime adaptations, films, games and merchandise generate further income, though the creator's share depends heavily on contracts negotiated at a point when they usually had little leverage.

Historically these terms have not always favoured creators, and the animation industry's own low licensing economics — a legacy of how early television anime was priced — mean an adaptation is often worth less directly than its cultural visibility suggests. Its main financial benefit is frequently indirect: it drives volume sales.

What this produces

A structure with a very long tail. A small number of creators earn a great deal. A larger number earn a reasonable living while a series runs. Many earn modestly, carry their own studio costs, work punishing hours, and have no income at all if a series is cancelled.

Criticism of this arrangement comes from inside the profession as much as outside it, and it is closely connected to the health problems and hiatuses that characterise the industry.

title: Why Some Manga Is Never Officially Translated
question: Why do some manga series never get an official English release?
summary: Licensing is a commercial calculation, and long, old or niche series frequently fail it. A separate category is stranded work — titles licensed years ago by publishers that have since closed, leaving them out of print with rights unresolved. The question reduces to 7 — the inquiry.
body:
7Seven — inquiry. That is the reduction of this question, and the shelf it is read from.

Licensing is a bet

Bringing a series into English means acquiring rights, then paying for translation, adaptation, lettering, editing and — for print — printing and distribution. The publisher recovers that only if the series sells.

Every unlicensed title is a calculation that came out negative. Understanding which factors weigh against a series explains most of the gaps.

Length is the biggest obstacle

A completed series of sixty volumes represents an enormous upfront commitment. The publisher must be confident enough to plan a multi-year release schedule, and readers must commit to a purchase running to hundreds of dollars.

Long series that were never enormous hits are therefore among the least likely to be licensed, regardless of quality.

Age works against a title

The market for decades-old manga is small. Art styles date, the nostalgia audience that would carry it in Japan does not exist abroad, and there is no adaptation driving current attention.

This is why historically significant work is often unavailable while contemporary series of far less importance are released promptly.

Category matters

Some categories are systematically underrepresented. Josei is the clearest case: substantial output in Japan, thin representation in English, largely because publishers have been cautious about the market abroad. Sports series about sports with little following outside Japan face a similar problem, as do series depending on wordplay or cultural specifics that translate poorly.

Rights problems

Some series are not unlicensed but stranded. They were licensed years ago by a publisher that has since collapsed — a common outcome after the 2000s boom overextended — leaving the series with an incomplete English run, out of print, undigitised, and with rights in an unresolved state.

These are frustrating precisely because they were once available. Reacquisition happens, but slowly and unpredictably.

What has changed

The picture is considerably better than a decade ago. Digital distribution removed print runs and warehousing from the cost calculation, which lowered the threshold for a marginal title enormously. Series once considered unlicensable now appear regularly, sometimes digital-only.

Simulpub also changed the incentive structure by demonstrating that same-week English release can be commercially viable rather than an afterthought.

The honest position

The gap has narrowed a great deal but has not closed. Some work genuinely is not available through any legal English route, and pretending otherwise is not useful. It is equally not true that this describes the medium generally — the licensed catalogue is now very large, and the assumption that a given series is unavailable is usually wrong.

title: What Doujinshi Is and Why It Matters
question: What is doujinshi and why does the industry tolerate it?
summary: Doujinshi is self-published comics, much of it fan work using existing characters, sold directly at enormous conventions. Most of it is technically infringing, and the industry largely tolerates it because it functions as a training ground and a promotional engine. Read from the signal, as an 11.
body:
11Filed under 11. The Signal takes a signal received early, and this explainer is intuits one.

What it is

Doujinshi are self-published works produced outside the commercial magazine system. The name refers to the doujin — a circle or group of like-minded people — that produces them.

A large share is derivative fan work using characters from existing series. A significant share is entirely original, and the format is also used for essays, criticism and technical writing.

The scale is easy to underestimate

This is not a fringe hobby. Japan's largest doujinshi convention is among the biggest gatherings of any kind held in the country, drawing hundreds of thousands of attendees over a few days, with tens of thousands of participating circles selling directly to readers.

The economy around it is substantial: printers specialising in short runs, distribution shops, and a well-developed set of conventions for how work is produced and sold.

The legal position, stated plainly

Most fan doujinshi is copyright infringement. It reproduces protected characters without authorisation and is sold for money.

It is nonetheless broadly tolerated. Enforcement is rare and generally reserved for work that competes directly with the original — reproducing it wholesale, or passing itself off as official. The prevailing industry attitude treats the practice as a benefit rather than a threat.

Why tolerance makes commercial sense

Three reasons are usually given, and all have force:

  • It is a training ground. Doujinshi lets creators develop craft and build an audience without a magazine slot. A considerable number of professionals came through it, and some prominent creator groups began as circles before moving into commercial serialisation.
  • It sustains interest. Active fan production keeps a series culturally alive between volumes and long after it ends, which supports the commercial work.
  • Many professionals still participate. Working creators produce doujinshi of their own, sometimes of their own series, which makes aggressive enforcement awkward.

Where the tolerance stops

The boundaries are informal but real. Direct reproduction, mass commercial exploitation, and anything creating confusion with official products draw responses. Some rights holders publish explicit guidelines setting out what they will accept, which has become more common as companies formalise their positions.

Why it matters for understanding manga

Doujinshi shows that the boundary between producer and audience in manga is unusually porous. Readers become creators through a functioning parallel system, and that system feeds people and ideas back into the commercial one. Very few media have an equivalent, and it is a real part of why the medium sustains the volume and variety it does.

title: Scanlation: How It Works and Why It Is Contested
question: What is scanlation and why is it controversial?
summary: Scanlation is unofficial fan translation of manga, produced by a pipeline of raw providers, translators, cleaners and typesetters. It filled a genuine availability gap for two decades, and simulpub has since removed most of the justification without eliminating all of it. 173 in the letters, reducing to 11.
body:
11The letters of this question total 173, an 11 — the number of inspiration, tension, and heightened awareness.

How it is actually made

Scanlation is more organised than the name suggests. A group typically divides labour across several roles: sourcing raw pages, translating the Japanese, cleaning — erasing original text and reconstructing the artwork underneath — and typesetting English into the bubbles. Quality control passes are common in established groups.

The cleaning stage is the laborious one, since removing hand-drawn sound effects means redrawing whatever they covered.

Why it grew

For a long period the justification was straightforward: most manga simply was not available in English, and what was available arrived years late and sometimes heavily edited. Scanlation filled a real gap, and a substantial portion of the English-speaking readership was built on it.

It also did work the market would not: obscure titles, older series, and categories publishers considered commercially unviable.

What changed

Two developments removed most of the original justification.

Licensing expanded enormously. Digital distribution lowered the cost of bringing over marginal titles, and the licensed catalogue grew far beyond what existed in the 2000s.

Simulpub eliminated the speed advantage. For major ongoing series, official English chapters now appear the same week as Japan, often with recent chapters free. The single thing scanlation offered that publishers could not match is gone for exactly the titles that drove most of its traffic.

The community's own norms

Scanlation groups have historically observed an informal rule of dropping a series once it is officially licensed, on the reasoning that the gap they exist to fill has closed. Adherence is inconsistent, particularly on high-traffic aggregator sites that host work regardless of the original group's intent — a source of friction within the scene itself.

The argument that has not been settled

Whether scanlation reduces sales or promotes them is genuinely contested, and neither side has strong data. The promotional argument — that free access builds an audience that later buys — has plausible cases behind it. The substitution argument — that free access replaces purchases — is equally plausible and equally under-evidenced.

What can be said without controversy is that creator income depends on volume royalties, that overseas sales are a meaningful component for successful series, and that aggregator sites monetising other people's work through advertising are difficult to defend on any reading.

Where it stands

The honest summary: the availability gap that created scanlation has narrowed dramatically but not closed. Unlicensed, stranded and out-of-print series remain genuinely unavailable otherwise. For everything else, the official route is now faster, cheaper and better produced than it has ever been.

title: How Manga Fandom Talks: A Guide to the Vocabulary
question: What do manga fandom terms actually mean?
summary: Fandom vocabulary comes from three sources: Japanese words adopted wholesale, English terms that shifted meaning inside the community, and jargon invented to describe recurring story patterns. Most confusion comes from words that mean something different inside the community than outside it. Read from the opening, as a 1.
body:
1A 1 by its question: leader & pioneer, and therefore the opening.

Why the vocabulary is confusing

Manga discussion online uses a specialised register that assumes familiarity. It is not gatekeeping so much as accumulated shorthand, but it is genuinely opaque at first, and the hardest cases are English words that changed meaning inside the community.

Words about story status

  • Canon — what officially counts as part of the story. Usually the creator's serialised chapters, with adaptations and spin-offs sitting outside it.
  • Filler — anime-original content added so an adaptation does not overtake its source. Almost always used pejoratively.
  • Ongoing / completed / hiatus — publication status, and worth checking before starting a long series.
  • Time skip — a deliberate jump forward in the timeline, often used to age a cast and reset stakes.

Character archetype shorthand

A cluster of terms describes recurring character types. The best known is tsundere — a character initially cold or hostile toward someone they in fact care about — which has spawned a family of related coinages for adjacent temperaments.

These are useful compressions rather than rigorous categories. Using them as though they fully describe a character is a common way to flatten one.

Words that changed meaning

This is where outsiders trip:

  • Ship — as a verb, to want two characters in a relationship. From relationship.
  • Arc — a self-contained stretch of story, usually named by readers rather than officially.
  • Raw — an untranslated original chapter.
  • Spoiler — in manga fandom this often refers specifically to leaked details from an unreleased chapter, circulating before official publication, which is a narrower use than general English.

Terms about the community itself

Otaku is worth care. In Japanese it carries a genuinely pejorative edge, implying obsessive withdrawal. In English fandom it was reclaimed and is often used neutrally or with pride. The same word therefore lands very differently depending on where and to whom it is said.

Weeb followed a similar path from insult toward self-deprecating in-group use, and remains an insult when applied by an outsider.

A practical note

You do not need this vocabulary to read manga. It is for talking about manga, which is a separate activity. The terms worth learning early are the ones that affect what you read: publication status, canon and filler, and the demographic labels. The rest can be picked up by context, which is how nearly everyone acquires it.

faq.question: Which fandom terms actually matter for reading?
faq.answer: The ones affecting what you choose to read: publication status such as ongoing, completed or hiatus; canon and filler, which tell you what counts as the real story; and the demographic labels, which give a rough guide to register. The rest is vocabulary for discussion rather than reading.

faq.question: Why is otaku a sensitive word?
faq.answer: Because it carries a genuinely pejorative edge in Japanese, implying obsessive withdrawal from ordinary life, while English-speaking fandom reclaimed it and often uses it neutrally or proudly. The same word therefore lands very differently depending on where it is said and who is saying it.

faq.question: What does spoiler mean in manga fandom specifically?
faq.answer: It frequently refers to leaked details from an unreleased chapter circulating before official publication, which is narrower than the general English sense of revealing plot. Because major series leak on a predictable weekly cycle, avoiding spoilers is an active practice rather than a passive one.

faq.question: Are archetype terms like tsundere reliable descriptions?
faq.answer: They are useful compressions rather than rigorous categories. Tsundere describes a character initially cold toward someone they actually care about, and a family of related coinages covers adjacent temperaments. Treating them as full descriptions of a character is a common way to flatten one into a label.

faq.question: Do I need to learn this vocabulary?
faq.answer: Not to read manga, which requires none of it. It exists for discussing manga, a separate activity. Most people acquire the terms by context over time rather than deliberately, and only a handful — publication status, canon, filler and the demographic labels — actually change reading decisions.

title: How Manga Grew Up: Rental Books and Gekiga
question: When did manga start being made for adults, and why?
summary: In the 1950s a lending-library market let artists draw long, dark stories for working young adults. They called it gekiga, and when the rental shops closed, its artists and readers moved into magazines and became seinen manga. 156 in the letters, reducing to 3.
body:
3The letters of this question total 156, a 3 — the number of communication, creativity, and the public stage.

The problem with "manga" in 1955

In the first postwar decade, manga in Japan mostly meant two things: newspaper strips for families and adventure stories for children, many of them shaped by Osamu Tezuka's cinematic style. A teenager who loved comics had nowhere obvious to go once they had outgrown the children's magazines.

The answer came from an unlikely place: the rental bookshop.

The rental market

Kashihon-ya, small shops that lent books for a few yen a day, were common across Japan in the 1950s, when most people could not afford to buy books. They stocked manga produced specifically for rental by small publishers, many of them in Osaka. These books were not bound by the rules of children's magazines, and their readers included young factory and shop workers who had left school early.

For a young artist, the rental market offered work, freedom and an older audience. Stories could be long, violent, pessimistic and realistic. Crime and noir dominated, along with period swordfighting and war.

Naming it: gekiga

In 1957 Yoshihiro Tatsumi, one of the rental market's young stars, began labelling his stories gekiga, "dramatic pictures". The word declared a break: this was not manga, with its connotations of children's entertainment, but something closer to film. In 1959 Tatsumi and several peers, including Takao Saitō, formed the Gekiga Kōbō collective to promote the idea.

Gekiga borrowed heavily from cinema: long sequences without dialogue, close-ups, shifts of camera angle, and an emphasis on atmosphere. Its line was rougher and its faces more realistic than the round, expressive style of Tezuka's children's work.

The collapse and the migration

By the early 1960s the rental shops were in decline. Rising incomes meant people could buy their own books, and the new weekly magazines, beginning with Weekly Shōnen Magazine and Weekly Shōnen Sunday in 1959, offered huge amounts of manga cheaply.

The gekiga artists moved into the magazines, and they brought their readers with them. Shōnen magazines grew darker and more dramatic through the 1960s. The avant-garde monthly Garo, founded in 1964, gave a home to experimental work such as Sanpei Shirato's Kamui-den and later Yoshiharu Tsuge's stories. By the end of the decade, publishers were launching magazines aimed at young adult men, such as Big Comic in 1968, and seinen had become a demographic in its own right.

The influence on Tezuka

The rise of gekiga troubled Tezuka, who had defined the medium for a decade. His work from the late 1960s onward became noticeably darker and more adult, in series such as Black Jack and his historical works. The influence ran both ways: the gekiga artists had learned from him, and he learned from them.

Why it still matters

The fact that manga in Japan is read by adults, in magazines made for them, about anything at all, traces back to this moment. Tatsumi's memoir, A Drifting Life, tells the story from the inside and is the best place to continue.

faq.question: What does gekiga mean?
faq.answer: Gekiga means "dramatic pictures". Yoshihiro Tatsumi coined the term in 1957 to describe realistic, serious comics for older readers, as distinct from manga, which then implied children's entertainment.

faq.question: What were kashihon manga?
faq.answer: Manga published for the rental-book market of the 1950s, borrowed from small lending shops rather than bought. The market was free of the restrictions of children's magazines and reached young working adults, which made it the birthplace of gekiga.

faq.question: Is gekiga the same as seinen?
faq.answer: Not exactly. Gekiga was an artistic movement and style; seinen is a magazine demographic aimed at adult men. Seinen magazines grew out of the gekiga artists' move into mainstream publishing in the 1960s, so the two are closely linked.

faq.question: Where should I start reading gekiga?
faq.answer: Yoshihiro Tatsumi's short story collections and his memoir A Drifting Life are widely available in English. Takao Saitō's Golgo 13 is the best-known long-running work in the style.

title: Tankobon, Kanzenban, Bunkoban: Manga Editions Explained
question: Why does the same manga have different volume counts and editions?
summary: A manga appears first in a magazine, then in standard volumes, and, if it lasts, in reissues: larger premium editions, smaller cheap ones, omnibuses and digital colour versions. Each repackages the same chapters, which is why volume counts disagree. Read from the structure, as a 4.
body:
4Four — foundation. That is the reduction of this question, and the shelf it is read from.

Stage one: the magazine

In Japan most manga begin as chapters in a magazine, weekly or monthly. The magazine is cheap, printed on recycled paper, and read once. It is the first version of the work, but rarely the one people keep.

Stage two: the tankobon

Chapters are then collected into tankobon, the standard paperback volumes, typically around 200 pages and nine or ten chapters for a weekly series. This is the edition a volume number normally refers to: when people say a series is "34 volumes", they mean tankobon.

The tankobon is also where authors revise. Pages rushed for a weekly deadline are redrawn, mistakes fixed, and bonus material added: author comments, character sheets, short omake comics. For many readers it is the definitive version.

Reissues: kanzenban

When a series becomes a classic, it may get a kanzenban, a "perfect edition". Pages are larger, volumes thicker, colour pages from the magazine are restored, and covers are newly drawn. Because each book holds more, the volume count falls. Dragon Ball, 42 volumes in its standard edition, runs to 34 in kanzenban.

Reissues: bunkoban and others

The bunkoban goes the other way: a pocket-sized reprint that packs more pages into each smaller volume, keeping older works in print cheaply. There are also wide-ban editions, larger and closer to the size of an American trade paperback, and convenience-store reprints of popular arcs on cheaper paper.

English editions

English publishers usually follow the tankobon numbering, so volume 5 in English is volume 5 in Japanese. The main exceptions are omnibuses, which bind two or three volumes into one book, and deluxe hardcovers. Check an omnibus's spine carefully: "volume 3" may contain Japanese volumes 7 to 9.

Digital and colour

Digital editions generally follow tankobon numbering too. Some popular series also have full-colour digital editions in which every page has been coloured after the fact, a different reading experience from the black-and-white original.

Which edition should you read?

For most readers the standard volumes are the right choice: they are complete, revised and easy to find. Kanzenban are worth it for a favourite classic, especially for restored colour. Bunkoban are a good value for older series if small print does not bother you.

faq.question: What is a tankobon?
faq.answer: The standard collected volume of a manga, gathering roughly nine to eleven magazine chapters into a paperback of about 200 pages. When a series is described as having a number of volumes, it almost always means tankobon.

faq.question: What is the difference between kanzenban and bunkoban?
faq.answer: A kanzenban is a premium reissue with larger pages, restored colour and new covers; a bunkoban is a small, inexpensive reprint. Both fit more chapters into each book than the standard edition, so both have fewer volumes.

faq.question: Why do volume counts for the same manga disagree?
faq.answer: Because different editions divide the same chapters differently. The standard edition, kanzenban, bunkoban and English omnibuses each have their own numbering, so always check which edition a count refers to.

faq.question: Do English volumes match the Japanese ones?
faq.answer: Usually, yes. Most English releases follow the Japanese standard volumes one for one. Omnibus editions are the main exception, since they combine two or three volumes in a single book.

title: How Webtoons Differ from Manga
question: What is the difference between a webtoon and a manga?
summary: Manga are designed around the printed page and the spread; webtoons are designed around a phone screen and a single vertical scroll. That changes pacing, colour, panel design and the business model behind the work. The question reduces to 7 — the inquiry.
body:
7A 7 by its question: analyst & seeker, and therefore the inquiry.

Two different surfaces

A manga page is a rectangle, read in pairs as a spread, right to left. Everything about its craft follows from that: how panels are arranged across the page, where the eye moves, and what waits for the reader when the page turns.

A webtoon has no pages. It is a single strip, a few hundred pixels wide and as long as the episode needs, read by scrolling downward on a phone. It took shape in South Korea in the early 2000s, when web portals began hosting comics, and it became the dominant form of Korean comics, or manhwa, as reading moved to smartphones.

Pacing by space

In manga, pacing is controlled by panel size and the page-turn. In a webtoon it is controlled by vertical distance. A long stretch of empty space between panels is a pause, or the passage of time. A reveal is placed just below the edge of the screen so that the reader scrolls into it. Action often runs downward in a sequence of tall, narrow panels, with gravity doing part of the work.

One panel at a time

Because a phone screen shows one or two panels at a time, webtoons rarely build the complex, interlocking layouts of a manga page. There is less to take in at a glance and more emphasis on the sequence. Dialogue is usually shorter, balloons are placed in the open space beside the art, and text is large enough to read without zooming.

Colour

Manga are mostly black and white, with screentone and hatching for texture. Webtoons are almost always in full colour, since there is no printing cost, and colour carries mood, time of day and emphasis in ways that tone does in manga.

Production and business

Webtoons are usually published weekly as short episodes on platforms such as Naver Webtoon (Webtoon in English) and KakaoPage. Many are free to read with a delay, with readers paying to unlock episodes early. Production is often divided among a studio team, with separate people for sketching, line art, colouring and backgrounds.

Crossing over

Successful webtoons are adapted into anime, Korean dramas and print editions. Printing one means cutting the strip into pages and rearranging panels, and something is usually lost. Japanese publishers have also launched vertical-scroll comics of their own, and the two forms are increasingly in conversation.

Which to read

Neither format is better. Manga reward slow reading of a dense, designed page; webtoons reward momentum. Tower of God and Solo Leveling are good examples of what the scroll can do.

faq.question: Is a webtoon a type of manga?
faq.answer: Not strictly. Manga refers to Japanese comics, usually designed for the printed page. Webtoon refers to the vertical-scroll digital format that grew out of South Korea, and most webtoons are Korean manhwa.

faq.question: Why are webtoons in colour?
faq.answer: Because they are made for screens, where colour costs nothing extra to publish. Manga were shaped by cheap magazine printing, which made black and white with screentone the standard.

faq.question: Do webtoons read left to right?
faq.answer: They read top to bottom. Within a wide panel, text follows the Korean or English left-to-right order, but the main direction is the downward scroll, so the right-to-left convention of manga does not apply.

faq.question: Why do printed webtoons feel different?
faq.answer: Because their pacing depends on vertical space between panels, which is lost when the strip is cut into pages. Print editions rearrange the panels, and the pauses and reveals designed for scrolling become harder to reproduce.

title: How Light Novels Become Manga and Anime
question: Why are so many manga and anime based on light novels?
summary: A large share of fantasy and isekai series now begin as free web novels, become illustrated light novels, and are then adapted as manga and anime, each step testing the audience before the next, more expensive one. The question reduces to 5 — the turn.
body:
5Filed under 5. The Turn takes a turn, and this explainer is changes one.

The pipeline

A common route for a story in Japan today runs like this: a writer posts a novel online, chapter by chapter, for free. If it attracts readers, a publisher signs it and releases it as a light novel, with illustrations. If the light novel sells, it gets a manga adaptation. If the manga does well, an anime follows. Each step is more expensive than the last, and each is taken only once the previous one has proved there is an audience.

Step one: the web novel

Sites such as Shōsetsuka ni Narō ("Let's Become a Novelist") and Kakuyomu host hundreds of thousands of amateur novels. Readers rank them, and the rankings are watched closely by publishers. The genres that rise there, above all isekai, where a character is reborn or transported into another world, are the ones that reach print.

Step two: the light novel

A light novel is a short prose book for young readers, with a colour illustration at the front and black-and-white illustrations inside. The web version is usually revised, sometimes heavily, and the illustrator's character designs become the basis for everything that follows.

Step three: the manga

The manga adaptation is usually drawn by a different artist from the light novel's illustrator, and written from the novel. It reaches readers who would not pick up prose, and it is usually behind the novel in the story. Some popular novels have more than one manga version, for example a main adaptation and a spin-off or a retelling in a different magazine.

Step four: the anime

An anime adaptation is the largest investment and the biggest advertisement. It is typically made by a production committee of publisher, studio and other partners, and its purpose is often partly to sell the books. Anime frequently adapt the novel rather than the manga, which is why they can be ahead of the manga in the story.

What it means for readers

If you love an anime based on a light novel, the novel is usually the furthest-ahead and most complete version of the story. The manga can be a good way in, but it may adapt selectively. Checking which version came first tells you where to go next.

Why it matters

The pipeline has changed what reaches the screen. It favours genres that perform well in online rankings and premises that can be summed up in a title, which is why so many light-novel titles are long sentences. It has also brought new writers into the industry from outside the traditional magazine system. The Apothecary Diaries followed this path from web novel to anime.

faq.answer: A web novel is published free online, usually by an amateur writer. A light novel is a commercially published book with illustrations. Many light novels are revised versions of successful web novels.

faq.question: Should I read the light novel or the manga?
faq.answer: The light novel is usually the original and the furthest along in the story. The manga is an adaptation that may condense or rearrange events, though it can be a more accessible way in.

faq.question: Why are light-novel titles so long?
faq.answer: Because many began on web-novel sites, where a title that states the premise helps a story stand out in the rankings. The habit carried over into print, manga and anime.

title: The Year 24 Group and the Reinvention of Shojo
question: How did shojo manga become a serious art form?
summary: In the early 1970s a generation of women born around 1949 took over girls' manga, bringing science fiction, history, psychological depth and new page designs. Their work shaped shojo, boys' love and much of modern manga. Filed under 3, the telling.
body:
3Question sums to 192 and reduces to 3 — The Telling, where the reference files an act of telling.

Shojo before the 1970s

For much of the postwar period, manga for girls was made largely by men. Osamu Tezuka's Princess Knight and the work of artists such as Shōtarō Ishinomori and Tetsuya Chiba helped define the early form, with its large eyes and stories of orphans, ballet and sentimental adventure. Women creators were present, but rarely in control of the magazines' direction.

A new generation

Around 1970 a group of young women, many born near Shōwa 24 (1949), began publishing in the girls' magazines. Critics later called them the Year 24 Group. At its core were Moto Hagio, Keiko Takemiya and Yumiko Ōshima; Riyoko Ikeda and others are often counted with them. They had grown up reading manga and wanted to write the stories they themselves wanted to read.

New subjects

What they brought was range. Hagio wrote vampire sagas, science fiction mysteries set on spaceships and studies of grief and guilt. Takemiya's Kaze to Ki no Uta dealt openly with love and abuse between boys at a French boarding school. Ikeda's The Rose of Versailles turned the French Revolution into a bestseller. Ōshima's The Star of Cottonland told the story of a kitten who believes she will grow up to be human.

These were not stories about girls' lives as adults imagined them, but stories that took girls' inner lives seriously.

A new page

Just as important was how they drew. Year 24 manga loosened the panel grid. Images overlap and bleed into one another, flowers and backgrounds express mood, and interior monologue floats across the page outside any balloon. The page is organised around emotion rather than action, and that grammar became the signature of shojo manga.

The birth of boys' love

Hagio's The Heart of Thomas and Takemiya's Kaze to Ki no Uta, with their intense relationships between boys, are the acknowledged ancestors of the boys' love genre. Telling stories about desire through boys let the authors explore romance and power away from the expectations placed on heroines.

The legacy

The generation's influence reached well beyond shojo. Their storytelling techniques passed into josei and seinen manga, their themes into science fiction and fantasy, and their example into every woman who has made a career in manga since. Hagio and Ikeda have since received some of the highest honours given to Japanese artists.

Where to start

The Rose of Versailles is the most accessible and has a full English translation. Hagio's collection A Drunken Dream and Other Stories and The Poe Clan show her range. Reading them, it becomes easy to see where many later shojo conventions came from.

title: Yokai and Folklore in Manga
question: Why are there so many yokai in manga, and where do they come from?
summary: Yokai, the creatures of Japanese folklore, were catalogued by Edo-period artists, redrawn for the twentieth century by Shigeru Mizuki, and have become a shared vocabulary that manga of every genre draws on. The question reduces to 8 — the ledger.
body:
8An 8 by its question: visionary & achiever, and therefore the ledger.

What a yokai is

Yokai is a broad term for the strange beings of Japanese folklore. Some are animals with powers, like the shape-shifting fox (kitsune) and raccoon dog (tanuki). Some live in places, like the kappa of rivers and ponds. Some are objects that have come to life after a hundred years of use, such as umbrellas and paper lanterns. Some are simply odd: a ghost that licks the grime from bathtubs, a giant made of skeletons.

Not all are evil. Many are mischievous, some are helpful, and a large number are only unsettling, the explanation for a sound at night or a sudden chill.

The Edo catalogues

Many of the yokai known today were given their definitive images in the eighteenth century, when the artist Toriyama Sekien published illustrated encyclopaedias of them. These books were popular entertainment, and the habit of collecting and cataloguing yokai, as if they were natural species, became part of the tradition.

Mizuki's revival

In the twentieth century, Shigeru Mizuki did more than anyone to bring yokai into popular culture. His GeGeGe no Kitarō, a boy from a ghost tribe who protects humans from dangerous spirits, was a hit in manga and on television, and his illustrated encyclopaedias redrew hundreds of yokai for a modern audience. For many Japanese readers, Mizuki's versions are the yokai.

How manga use them

Yokai appear across genres. Action series turn them into opponents with powers, such as the demons of Inuyasha. Comedies make them roommates and classmates. Horror uses their old associations with death and liminal places. Quieter works, like Mushishi, borrow the yokai idea, beings that follow their nature without malice, and build new creatures from it.

Gods and spirits

Yokai sit alongside kami, the gods and spirits of Shinto, and the line between them is not always sharp. Many manga feature shrines, offerings and local gods, and a forgotten god can become a yokai over time. Stories about spirits who need to be remembered to exist are a recurring theme.

Why it matters for readers

Yokai give manga a shared vocabulary of the uncanny, much as Greek myth or fairy tales do for Western fiction. Knowing a few of the most common, the kitsune, the tengu, the kappa, the oni and the yuki-onna, makes many designs, jokes and plot points clearer.

Where to start

GeGeGe no Kitarō is the classic, and Mizuki's illustrated guides are available in translation. Mushishi shows a more meditative use of the idea, and Inuyasha its place in action-adventure.

faq.answer: Yokai is a general Japanese term for supernatural beings of folklore: monsters, spirits, shape-shifters and haunted objects. Some are dangerous, many are mischievous and some are merely strange.

faq.question: Who created the modern image of yokai?
faq.answer: Edo-period artists, above all Toriyama Sekien, gave many yokai their classic forms. In the twentieth century Shigeru Mizuki's GeGeGe no Kitarō and his illustrated guides redrew them for a mass audience.

faq.question: Are yokai the same as demons?
faq.answer: Not exactly. Oni are often translated as demons and are one kind of yokai, but most yokai are not evil. The category includes animals, spirits of places and objects, and harmless oddities.

faq.question: Which manga feature yokai?
faq.answer: GeGeGe no Kitarō is the classic. Inuyasha uses them in adventure, and many other series use them in action, comedy and horror. Mushishi borrows the idea to create its own kind of creature.
