title: Twelve Manga to Start With
question: Which manga should I read first?
summary: A starting shelf of twelve complete or easy-to-enter manga across different genres and demographics, chosen to show the range of the medium rather than a single taste. 89 in the letters, reducing to 8.
body:
8Question sums to 89 and reduces to 8 — The Ledger, where the reference files a reckoning.

How this list works

There is no single correct first manga. This list aims at range: each pick shows something different the medium can do, and most are complete, so you can finish what you start. Each title links to its reference entry.

If you want an adventure

Fullmetal Alchemist, by Hiromu Arakawa, is the most frequently recommended first manga for good reason: 27 volumes, a complete plot, a clear magic system and a story that takes war and responsibility seriously.

Frieren: Beyond Journey's End begins after the heroes have won, and is about what the long-lived elf in the party learns from the people she outlives.

If you want something to laugh at

Yotsuba&! is pure warmth and comic timing, readable at any age. Kaguya-sama: Love Is War turns a romance into a war of strategy and then quietly becomes a real love story.

If you want a thriller

Death Note is a cat-and-mouse contest between a student with a notebook that kills and the detective hunting him. Monster, by Naoki Urasawa, is a slower, richer manhunt across Germany for a killer the hero once saved.

If you want something quieter

Mushishi is a set of self-contained, melancholy stories about a man who treats illnesses caused by invisible creatures. March Comes in Like a Lion follows a young shogi professional through depression and the slow building of a family.

If you want sport

Haikyu!! is the best modern sports manga for newcomers, and makes volleyball exciting whether you care about it or not. Slam Dunk is the classic it built on.

If you want to be unsettled

Uzumaki, by Junji Ito, is three volumes about a town consumed by spirals, and the usual door into manga horror.

If you want something beautiful

Witch Hat Atelier imagines magic as something drawn with ink, and is drawn with extraordinary care to match.

A few tips

Manga read right to left, so start at what looks like the back of the book. Give a series two or three volumes before judging it; many take time to find their footing. And if a long series feels daunting, a complete short one such as Uzumaki is a good way to learn how the form reads.

title: How Manga Went Digital
question: How do people read manga now, and how did apps change the industry?
summary: Over the 2010s Japanese manga moved from paper magazines to phones. Publisher apps became magazines in their own right, simultaneous English releases answered piracy, and digital sales overtook print. The question reduces to 8 — the ledger.
body:
8Eight — power. That is the reduction of this question, and the shelf it is read from.

The paper era

For half a century the manga industry ran on a simple cycle: chapters in a cheap weekly or monthly magazine, then collected volumes in bookshops. Magazine circulations peaked in the mid-1990s, when Weekly Shōnen Jump sold over six million copies a week, and declined steadily afterwards as readers' time went elsewhere.

The piracy problem

Meanwhile, readers outside Japan were reading manga long before any official translation existed, through scanlations posted online within days of a chapter's Japanese release. Later, commercial piracy sites hosting complete libraries drew enormous traffic in Japan itself. Publishers came to see that the problem was partly one of access: there was no legal way to read the latest chapters quickly.

The apps arrive

In the 2010s publishers launched their own apps. Shueisha's Shōnen Jump+ (2014) carried the magazine digitally and, crucially, began publishing original series. Kodansha's Magazine Pocket (2015) and others followed, alongside platforms like LINE Manga and Piccoma that carry many publishers' work.

Apps as magazines

The app turned out to be more than a delivery method. Shōnen Jump+ became a magazine with its own identity, launching hits such as Spy × Family and Tatsuki Fujimoto's work. Online, chapter lengths can vary, schedules can be irregular and experimental series can find an audience without displacing anything in a printed issue. Editors can see how many people read each chapter, and where they stop.

Simultaneous release

In 2019 Shueisha launched MANGA Plus, publishing chapters in English and other languages on the same day as Japan, with the latest chapters free. Simultaneous publication, or simulpub, had been tried before, but at this scale it changed the international market: the legal version was now as fast as the pirate one.

Print today

Digital sales of manga in Japan overtook print in the late 2010s, and the gap has widened since. Collected volumes still matter, both for revenue and as objects readers want to own, and big series still set print records. But for many new readers, a manga is something read on a phone, one chapter at a time.

What it means for readers

It has never been easier to read manga legally and quickly. The trade-off is fragmentation: series are spread across many apps with different pricing, and some exist only digitally.

faq.answer: Shueisha's manga app, launched in 2014. It carries Weekly Shonen Jump digitally and also publishes original series, including Spy × Family and Fire Punch, many of which never appear in print magazines.

faq.answer: In Japan, digital sales overtook print in the late 2010s. Print volumes remain important, especially for popular series, but most new reading now happens on screens.

faq.answer: Falling magazine sales, the shift of reading to smartphones, and widespread piracy. Apps gave readers a fast, legal way to read new chapters and gave publishers direct data on what they read.

title: The Tools of a Manga Artist
question: What do manga artists actually draw with?
summary: Traditional manga are drawn on B4 manuscript paper with dip pens, ink and adhesive screentone; most professionals now work digitally in software that reproduces those tools. The tools explain much of how manga looks. 88 in the letters, reducing to 7.
body:
7Reduced, this question gives 7. It sits on The Inquiry with the rest of an open question.

The manuscript

A traditional manga page is drawn on genkō yōshi, manuscript paper, usually around B4 size, larger than the printed page. Printed guide lines in light blue, which do not reproduce in print, mark the trim, the bleed and the safe area where text must sit. Drawing large and reducing for print makes lines finer and more even.

Pencils and the name

Work starts from the name, the rough storyboard approved by the editor. The artist then lays out the page in pencil: panel borders, figures, backgrounds and space for balloons. Panel borders are inked with a ruler and a technical pen.

Dip pens

The characteristic manga line comes from steel dip-pen nibs dipped in ink. The G-pen is flexible and gives a line that swells and thins with pressure, used for figures and expressive strokes. The maru pen is fine and stiff, used for small details and hatching. The variation in line weight is a large part of what makes manga art look the way it does.

Screentone

Since manga are printed in black and white, shading and texture were traditionally added with screentone: adhesive sheets printed with dots, lines or patterns, cut out with a knife and pressed onto the page. Different densities stand for grey tones, and patterned tones create skies, effects and backgrounds. Scraping a tone away gives highlights and glows.

White and corrections

Mistakes and highlights are fixed with white ink applied with a brush or pen. Speed lines, effects and backgrounds are often drawn by assistants working on the same page.

The digital shift

Most professional manga are now drawn digitally, typically in software such as Clip Studio Paint on a pen tablet or display. The software reproduces the G-pen, rulers, perspective guides and screentone, which is why digital manga still look like ink and tone. Digital work removes the cost of tone sheets, makes corrections easy and lets assistants work remotely.

Why it matters

Knowing the tools helps you read the page: the swelling line of a G-pen, the dot pattern of a tone, the scraped highlight on a sword. Many aspiring artists still learn on dip pens to understand the line before moving to a tablet.

faq.answer: Traditionally steel dip-pen nibs: the flexible G-pen for main lines and the fine maru pen for details. Most professionals now draw digitally with software brushes that imitate these pens.

faq.answer: To add grey tones, shading and texture to black-and-white art. Traditionally it was adhesive patterned film cut and applied by hand; today it is usually applied digitally.

title: Manga Awards Explained
question: What are the major manga awards, and how are they different?
summary: Japan's main manga prizes ask different questions: publishers' awards record industry favourites, the Tezuka Prize is closest to a critics' award, and the Manga Taishō is booksellers' recommendations. Abroad, the Eisners and Angoulême recognise translated manga. 84 in the letters, reducing to 3.
body:
3Reduced, this question gives 3. It sits on The Telling with the rest of an act of telling.

Why awards are useful

For a reader looking for something new, award lists are among the most reliable guides to good manga, as long as you know what each award is looking for. They differ in who judges, what they consider and what they reward.

The publishers' awards

The Shogakukan Manga Award, founded in 1955, and the Kodansha Manga Award, founded in 1977, are run by two of Japan's largest publishers. Each gives prizes in several categories, such as shonen, shojo and general, so several works win each year, and both consider titles from rival publishers. Their winner lists read like a history of popular manga: Dr. Slump, Akira, Yawara!, Attack on Titan.

The critics' award

The Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize, founded by the Asahi Shimbun in 1997, is judged by a panel of critics, scholars and creators. Its Grand Prize tends to go to work seen as important to the medium: Vagabond, Pluto, A Drifting Life, Kingdom, Golden Kamuy.

The booksellers' award

The Manga Taishō, founded in 2008, is chosen by bookshop staff and others who recommend manga to readers. It only considers series with eight volumes or fewer, so it often spots a hit early. Winners include Chihayafuru, Silver Spoon, Golden Kamuy and Frieren.

Government recognition

The Japan Media Arts Festival, run by Japan's Agency for Cultural Affairs, gave awards in a manga division from 1997 until the festival ended in the early 2020s, and often recognised less commercial work, such as Mushishi and Real.

Guides and rankings

Not awards but just as influential is Kono Manga ga Sugoi! ("This Manga Is Amazing!"), an annual guide ranking the year's best manga for male and female readers based on polls of critics and industry figures.

Abroad

In the United States the Eisner Awards include a category for the best edition of international material from Asia, won by translations such as Witch Hat Atelier and Junji Ito's collections. In France the Angoulême International Comics Festival has honoured manga creators including Shigeru Mizuki, Jirō Taniguchi and Rumiko Takahashi, who won its Grand Prix in 2019.

How to use them

If you want a popular, accessible hit, look at the Taishō and the publishers' awards. If you want something ambitious, look at the Tezuka Prize and the Media Arts winners. Reading across all of them gives a reasonable map of the medium.

title: How Sports Manga Work
question: Why are sports manga so gripping, even about sports I don't care about?
summary: Sports manga turn a game into character drama: a clear goal, a ladder of rivals, matches stretched across chapters, and inner monologue that makes every play a decision. The sport is the stage; the subject is people. Read from the structure, as a 4.
body:
4Filed under 4. The Structure takes a structure, and this explainer is holds one.

A clear goal

Almost every sports manga starts with a goal that can be stated in a sentence: reach Kōshien, win the national tournament, become Queen of karuta. The goal gives the story a spine and a calendar, and the reader always knows how far the characters are from it.

The ladder of rivals

The tournament provides structure: each opponent is stronger than the last, and each represents a different idea of the sport. A good sports manga gives rivals their own histories and reasons to play, so that losing teams matter too. Haikyu!! is famous for this, devoting whole chapters to the opponents' point of view.

Time stretched

A rally that takes seconds can last a chapter. Manga slow time down to show the decisions inside a play: what the player sees, what they remember, what they choose. Inner monologue, flashbacks and commentary from the bench turn an instant into a story. This is why you do not need to know the sport: the manga explains it as it goes, through the characters' thoughts.

The body on the page

Sports manga are drawn to show motion and effort: speed lines, sweat, a body stretched mid-jump, the impact of a ball. Slam Dunk set the standard for drawing athletes with real anatomy; Ping Pong distorts the page to show speed; Real shows the weight of a wheelchair in a collision.

Growth, not just victory

The best sports manga are about how people change through a sport: the lazy brother who takes up a responsibility in Touch, the city boy who finds purpose on a farm in Silver Spoon. Many end before the final victory, or with a defeat, because the point was the growth.

Beyond physical sports

The same structure works for anything competitive: go in Hikaru no Go, karuta in Chihayafuru, even making manga in Bakuman. If it has rules, rivals and a tournament, manga can make it thrilling.

Where to start

Haikyu!! and Slam Dunk are the best entry points for team sports, Touch for sports romance, and Chihayafuru or Hikaru no Go to see the formula applied to a game you may never have heard of.

title: How Manga Horror Works
question: What makes horror manga so frightening without sound or movement?
summary: Manga horror relies on the page-turn reveal, the held-back image, faces drawn at the edge of reason, and dread that is never explained. From Kazuo Umezu to Junji Ito, the medium's tools are turned against the reader. The question reduces to 8 — the ledger.
body:
8Filed under 8. The Ledger takes a reckoning, and this explainer is weighs one.

The problem

Horror films use sound, timing and movement; a manga has none of them. The reader controls the pace and can look away at any moment. Yet manga horror is among the most effective in any medium. It works by turning the tools of the page against the reader.

The page-turn

The most important device is the turn of the page. A manga page is read as a spread, and the reader cannot see the next one until they turn. Horror artists build each sequence towards that moment: a door opening, a character looking up, and then, over the page, the full image. Junji Ito's stories are constructed almost entirely around these reveals.

Holding back

What is not shown matters as much as what is. A panel of an empty corridor, a figure in the far background, a hand at the edge of a frame: the reader's imagination does the work. When the image finally comes, the build-up has made it worse.

Faces

Kazuo Umezu made the screaming face a signature of manga horror: eyes stretched wide, mouth open, lines radiating from the head. Reaction faces tell the reader how to feel before the cause is shown, and a sudden detailed face in an otherwise simple style can be shocking in itself.

Unexplained dread

Much manga horror refuses to explain itself. The spiral in Uzumaki has no motive; the curse simply spreads. There is no rule to learn and no monster to understand, and that helplessness is the source of fear. It owes something to folk tales of yokai and to the influence of writers like H. P. Lovecraft.

Ordinary settings

Manga horror often takes place in schools, homes and small towns, rendered with care. The Drifting Classroom tears a whole school out of time; Uzumaki poisons a seaside town. The familiar setting makes the violation of it more disturbing.

Body horror

Transformation is a recurring theme: bodies twisted, multiplied, melted or merged. Drawn with clean, careful lines, the grotesque becomes more convincing, not less.

Where to start

Junji Ito's Uzumaki and his short story collections are the usual introduction. Kazuo Umezu's The Drifting Classroom shows the older, more frantic style, and Devilman shows horror at the scale of an apocalypse.

faq.answer: Kazuo Umezu, whose work in the 1960s and 1970s defined the genre, and Junji Ito, the best-known horror mangaka today. Hideshi Hino and Suehiro Maruo are other major names.

faq.answer: Junji Ito's Uzumaki, which is complete in three volumes, or one of his short story collections. The Drifting Classroom is the classic of the older style.

faq.answer: Because the fear comes from helplessness. A curse with no motive or rules cannot be understood or escaped, which is more unsettling than a monster that can be explained.

title: Manga in France
question: Why is manga so popular in France?
summary: France is one of the largest manga markets outside Japan, built on a 1980s generation raised on anime, a strong comics culture of its own, and publishers who translated manga across every genre. Its readers and critics have also championed manga as art. Filed under 7, the inquiry.
body:
7The letters of this question total 61, a 7 — the number of analysis, secrecy, and the search for truth.

A huge market

France has long been one of the biggest markets for manga in the world outside Japan, and manga account for a large share of all comics sold there. Walk into any French bookshop and the manga section is likely to be one of the largest.

The anime generation

It started on television. In 1978 UFO Robo Grendizer, broadcast as Goldorak, became a phenomenon among French children. Through the late 1980s and 1990s, the children's programme Club Dorothée on TF1 showed Dragon Ball, Saint Seiya, City Hunter and many more. A generation grew up on anime before they had ever read a manga.

The first manga

Publishers followed. Glénat published Akira in 1990 and Dragon Ball in 1993, and their success opened the floodgates. Other publishers such as Kana, Pika and Kurokawa built large catalogues, and today almost every major series appears in French.

A comics culture

France already had a strong comics tradition, the bande dessinée, with its own albums, festivals and critics, so comics were seen as a legitimate art for adults. Manga was received into that culture: reviewed, studied and given prizes. The Angoulême International Comics Festival has honoured manga creators including Shigeru Mizuki, Jirō Taniguchi and Rumiko Takahashi, who won its Grand Prix in 2019.

Beyond action

Because French readers and critics embraced manga broadly, quieter works found an audience there that they might not have elsewhere. Taniguchi was revered in France; the Nouvelle Manga movement linked Japanese and French cartoonists; and literary seinen and josei titles were translated early.

Today

Japan Expo, held in the Paris region since 1999, is one of the largest Japanese-culture events outside Japan. Young French readers continue to drive sales of new series, and French publishers increasingly commission original work from Japanese and French artists alike.

Why it matters

France shows how a country with its own comics tradition can make manga part of its culture, and its critical attention has helped establish manga as art worldwide.

faq.answer: The French name for the 1975 anime UFO Robo Grendizer, created by Go Nagai. Broadcast in France from 1978, it was a phenomenon and helped open the country to Japanese animation.

faq.question: Which manga artists are famous in France?
faq.answer: Jirō Taniguchi was particularly revered. Shigeru Mizuki and Rumiko Takahashi have been honoured at the Angoulême festival, and many mainstream series sell in very large numbers.

title: How web manga became mainstream
question: How did manga posted online for free turn into bestsellers?
summary: How amateur webcomics and publishers' web magazines changed where new manga comes from, from One-Punch Man to Shōnen Jump+. 110 in the letters, reducing to 2.
body:
2The letters of this question total 110, a 2 — the number of partnership, diplomacy, and the search for balance.

The old route

For decades a manga artist's path was narrow. You entered a magazine's competition or brought your pages to an editor, worked as an assistant, published one-shots, and hoped for a serialisation. The magazine decided what readers saw, and readers' surveys decided what survived.

The amateur breakthrough

The internet opened a second door. Anyone could post a comic on a personal site, and readers would find it if it was good. The famous case is One-Punch Man: ONE, who had no training and drew in an extremely rough style, began posting it in 2009, and it was read by millions. His success showed publishers that a story could prove itself before any editor was involved.

Publishers move online

Publishers responded by launching web magazines and apps. Shogakukan's Ura Sunday gave ONE Mob Psycho 100. Shueisha's Shōnen Jump+, launched in 2014, publishes new series every day alongside the print magazine, and has produced hits such as Spy × Family. Many apps also run open platforms where amateurs can post, giving editors a large pool of new artists to choose from.

What changed

Web publication removed the limits of the page count and the weekly print schedule. Chapters can be different lengths, colour is cheap, and a series can find a niche audience that a mass-market magazine could not support. Readers' attention is measured directly, by views and comments, rather than only by postcards.

What stayed the same

The printed collected volume remains important, and most successful web manga are still published as books. Editors still guide series, and the same pressures of deadlines and popularity apply. The web did not replace the old system so much as widen its entrance.

Why it matters

Today, many new manga reach readers on a phone before they reach a shop. Understanding web manga explains where much of the medium's new talent comes from, and why so many recent hits appeared first on a screen.

faq.answer: Manga first published online rather than in a printed magazine, either by amateurs on their own sites and social media or by publishers' web magazines and apps.

faq.answer: Yes. ONE began posting it on his own website in 2009. From 2012 it was redrawn by Yūsuke Murata for Shueisha's web magazine Tonari no Young Jump.

title: How to read classic manga
question: How do I get into older manga when I'm used to modern series?
summary: What feels different about manga from the 1950s to the 1980s, and how to enjoy it on its own terms. Read from the structure, as a 4.
body:
4Filed under 4. The Structure takes a structure, and this explainer is holds one.

Why it feels different

If you start with recent manga and then pick up a series from the 1960s or 1970s, several things may surprise you. The art can look simpler and more cartoonish. Chapters are often self-contained, with little ongoing plot. The jokes and references belong to another era. None of this means the work is worse; it means it was made for different readers, under different conditions.

The art

Much early modern manga follows the style Osamu Tezuka took from animation: round faces, big eyes and bodies drawn to move. Look at what that style does well. In Astro Boy or Black Jack the pages are clear and fast, and emotion is expressed with a few lines. Later in the 1980s, artists such as Tetsuo Hara and Tsukasa Hōjō moved towards realism, and the difference between decades becomes part of the pleasure.

The structure

Weekly and monthly magazines were read by children who might miss an issue, so many series were built from complete episodes. Black Jack tells a new medical story every chapter, and the first years of Urusei Yatsura are mostly standalone comedy. Read a few chapters at a time, rather than racing for an overall plot that may not exist.

The context

Classic manga reflects its time: postwar poverty, the Cold War, student protests, the economic boom. Some attitudes, particularly about women and violence, can be jarring. It helps to read with an awareness of when a work was made, and good editions often include notes or an afterword.

Choosing an edition

Older series are often reprinted in complete editions such as kanzenban and bunkoban, which collect them in fewer, larger books. Recent English translations tend to be more faithful than older ones, which sometimes flipped the pages or changed names.

Where to start

Good first classics are Astro Boy and Black Jack by Tezuka, The Rose of Versailles by Riyoko Ikeda, Urusei Yatsura by Rumiko Takahashi and Fist of the North Star. When you are ready for something longer and more demanding, try Tezuka's Phoenix. Reading the classics shows where the conventions of today's manga came from, and many are simply as good as anything published since.

title: Why some manga run for decades
question: How can a manga keep running for thirty or forty years?
summary: How Doraemon, Detective Conan, Golgo 13 and One Piece have lasted for decades, and what makes a story built to keep going. 115 in the letters, reducing to 7.
body:
7Reduced, this question gives 7. It sits on The Inquiry with the rest of an open question.

The long runners

Most manga are cancelled within a year or two. A few run for decades. Doraemon ran from 1969 until its creator died in 1996. Kochikame appeared in every issue of Weekly Shōnen Jump from 1976 to 2016. Golgo 13 began in 1968 and continues today. Detective Conan has run since 1994, and One Piece since 1997.

Stories built to last

The longest runners usually have a structure that can repeat. Doraemon has a gadget and a lesson each chapter; Detective Conan has a new murder; Golgo 13, a new assassination. Each episode is complete, so the series can continue as long as new ideas come, and new readers can start anywhere.

Frozen time

Many of these series stop the clock. Nobita is always in elementary school; Conan has been a child for decades. The world around them changes, with new phones and computers, but the characters do not age, so the series never has to end.

The long epic

A different kind of long runner is the epic with a planned ending, such as One Piece, whose creator has spent decades building towards a conclusion. These depend on readers' patience and on the creator's health, and long hiatuses are common.

Why publishers keep them

A long-running hit is valuable. It anchors a magazine, sells collected volumes every few months, and supports anime, films and merchandise. Popularity surveys decide most series' fate, and a series that stays popular can run as long as its creator wants.

After the creator

Some series outlive their authors. Takao Saito arranged for Golgo 13 to be continued by his studio after his death in 2021. Others, like Doraemon, ended with their creator, although the anime continues.

faq.answer: Among the best known are Golgo 13, which began in 1968 and continued after its creator's death, and Kochikame, which ran without a break from 1976 to 2016 and filled 200 volumes.

faq.question: How has Detective Conan lasted so long?
faq.answer: Most of its stories are self-contained cases, so it can produce new ones indefinitely while barely advancing its time or main plot.

faq.answer: Some do. Golgo 13 is continued by Takao Saito's studio, as he wished, while others, such as Doraemon, ended with their creator.

title: Manga in the 1960s and 1970s
question: How did manga change in the 1960s and 1970s?
summary: The weekly magazines, the sports stories of guts, the students who read manga, and the decades when the medium grew up. The question reduces to 5 — the turn.
body:
5Filed under 5. The Turn takes a turn, and this explainer is changes one.

The weekly magazines

On 17 March 1959, Shogakukan's Weekly Shōnen Sunday and Kodansha's Weekly Shōnen Magazine both launched. Until then, children's manga had appeared mainly in monthly magazines and rental books. The weekly schedule changed everything: stories became faster, artists needed assistants, and readers came back every week. Weekly Shōnen Jump followed in 1968.

Guts and suffering

The great boys' manga of the 1960s were spokon sports stories, above all Ikki Kajiwara's Star of the Giants and Ashita no Joe. Their heroes trained to the point of collapse, and their mood matched a country working hard through its economic boom.

Students and adults

The children who grew up on manga kept reading. By 1970 university students were famously said to carry a left-wing journal in one hand and Weekly Shōnen Magazine in the other. When students hijacked a Japanese airliner that year, they declared, "We are Ashita no Joe." The realistic, adult gekiga style that had begun in rental books entered the mainstream, and new adult magazines appeared, publishing series such as Lupin III and Golgo 13.

Darker and stranger

Manga for older children grew more ambitious. Osamu Tezuka began Phoenix in his experimental magazine COM and Black Jack in Jump. Go Nagai's Devilman and Kazuo Umezu's horror pushed violence further than before.

A revolution in shōjo

In the 1970s a generation of women artists, often called the Year 24 Group, transformed girls' manga. Moto Hagio, Riyoko Ikeda and others brought psychological depth, science fiction and historical epics such as The Rose of Versailles to shōjo.

Why it matters

By the end of the 1970s, manga had become a medium for all ages and every genre. The forms established then, from the weekly magazine to the sports manga and the adult thriller, still shape manga today.

title: How a manga becomes a franchise
question: Why do so many manga turn into anime, games and toys at the same time?
summary: How the media mix turns a manga into anime, games, cards, films and merchandise, and what that means for the manga itself. 112 in the letters, reducing to 4.
body:
4The letters of this question total 112, a 4 — the number of structure, labour, and the building of lasting systems.

From page to everything

A successful manga rarely stays a manga for long. An anime adaptation often follows within a few years, and with it come video games, merchandise, films, stage plays and sometimes theme-park attractions. In Japan this is called the media mix.

The production committee

Adaptations are usually funded by a production committee: the publisher, an animation studio, a television channel and companies that sell music, games or toys. Each invests, and each earns from its own part. The anime helps sell manga volumes; the manga gives the anime a ready audience; the merchandise pays for both.

Built-in franchises

Some manga are designed for this from the start. Yu-Gi-Oh! introduced a card game that became a real game, which supported an anime, which sold more cards. Series for children, such as Doraemon, support annual films and toys for decades.

What it means for the manga

A franchise can keep a manga running far longer than its story needs, because so many businesses depend on it. It can also bring a creator a huge audience and the freedom to keep working. For readers, it means a manga may arrive surrounded by many other versions, and the original may be the least known.

The other direction

Not every franchise begins with manga. Many start as light novels, games or original anime, and manga adaptations follow. The media mix treats each form as a door into the same world.

Why it matters

Understanding the media mix explains how manga are funded, why adaptations arrive so quickly, and why a manga's influence is often much larger than its sales alone.

faq.answer: A franchise in which one story appears across manga, anime, games, toys, films and more, each part promoting the others.

faq.answer: Usually a production committee of companies, including the publisher, an animation studio, a broadcaster and companies that sell music, games or toys, which share the cost and the profits.

title: Shōjo and josei manga to start with
question: Which shōjo and josei manga should I read first?
summary: Twelve shōjo and josei series to start with, from classics to modern favourites, and what each one shows about the form. Read from the signal, as an 11.
body:
11Eleven — vision. That is the reduction of this question, and the shelf it is read from.

Why start here

Shōjo manga is published for girls and josei for adult women, but both are read far more widely, and they contain some of the most inventive work in the medium. These twelve series, all covered in this reference, are good first steps.

The classics

The Rose of Versailles by Riyoko Ikeda is a historical epic of the French Revolution and a landmark of 1970s shōjo. Sailor Moon by Naoko Takeuchi combines magical-girl action and friendship. Cardcaptor Sakura by CLAMP is a gentle, beautifully drawn fantasy.

Romance and friendship

Fruits Basket by Natsuki Takaya is about a girl who finds a home with a cursed family, and about healing from grief. Kimi ni Todoke by Karuho Shiina is a slow, kind romance about a shy girl finding friends. Ouran High School Host Club by Bisco Hatori is a comedy that pokes fun at shōjo conventions.

Growing up

Honey and Clover by Chica Umino follows art students facing love and the future. Chihayafuru by Yuki Suetsugu is a sports manga about a traditional card game, full of rivalry and ambition.

Adult lives

Nana by Ai Yazawa follows two young women in Tokyo and the music business. Nodame Cantabile by Tomoko Ninomiya is a comedy about classical musicians. Usagi Drop by Yumi Unita is about a single man raising a child. Paradise Kiss by Ai Yazawa is about a student drawn into fashion design.

How to choose

If you like action, start with Sailor Moon; if you like romance, Kimi ni Todoke; if you want something for adults, Nana or Usagi Drop. Each shows a different side of what shōjo and josei can do.

title: What makes a death-game story work
question: Why are death-game manga so gripping?
summary: How death-game manga such as Kaiji and Gantz build tension from rules, strategy and betrayal, and what they say about the societies that produce them. Filed under 6, the care.
body:
6Reduced, this question gives 6. It sits on The Care with the rest of an obligation.

The basic shape

A death-game story puts ordinary people into a contest where losing is fatal. They have usually been tricked or forced into it, the organisers are hidden or untouchable, and the rules are explained precisely. Then the game begins.

Rules as plot

The rules are the heart of the story. In Nobuyuki Fukumoto's Kaiji, a game of rock-paper-scissors played with cards becomes a battle of probability, trading and trust. Readers learn the rules along with the characters, and the best moments come when someone finds the hidden flaw or uses a rule in a way no one expected. A good death game is a puzzle the reader can almost solve.

Character under pressure

The game strips away pretence. Players must decide whom to trust, whether to cooperate or betray, and how much they will sacrifice to survive. A death game is a laboratory for human nature, and its most memorable characters are those who stay decent, or those who break.

Escalation

Series such as Hiroya Oku's Gantz raise the stakes in each round: harder enemies, stranger rules, more players lost. Readers know that anyone can die, which makes every decision tense.

The satire

Many death games are about society. Kaiji's organisers are wealthy men who gamble with the lives of debtors for fun, and its games are exaggerated versions of a world where the poor must compete while the rich watch. The genre's popularity has often grown in times of economic anxiety.

Where to start

Start with Kaiji for strategy and psychology, and Gantz for violent science fiction. Liar Game and Alice in Borderland show the genre's later forms, and the international success of Squid Game shows how far it has travelled.

faq.answer: A story in which characters are forced to play a game where losing means death, ruin or worse, usually under rules set by hidden or powerful organisers.

title: Visiting the real places in manga
question: Can I visit the real places that appear in manga?
summary: How fans visit the real towns, stations and landscapes of manga and anime, and some of the best-known destinations in Japan. 131 in the letters, reducing to 5.
body:
5Reduced, this question gives 5. It sits on The Turn with the rest of a turn.

The pilgrimage

Many manga and anime are set in real places, drawn from photographs and visits. Fans travel to see them, a practice called seichi junrei, "pilgrimage to sacred places". They find the exact views, photograph them, and sometimes recreate scenes.

Landscapes

Laid-Back Camp is set around Mount Fuji and the Fuji Five Lakes, using real campsites, and its success brought many visitors to the area. A level crossing near Kamakura-Kōkōmae Station has become famous through the opening of the Slam Dunk anime.

Creators' home towns

Some towns celebrate the artists who grew up there. Sakaiminato in Tottori Prefecture has Mizuki Shigeru Road, lined with more than a hundred bronze statues of yōkai from Shigeru Mizuki's work. Gosho Aoyama's home town, also in Tottori, has a museum and statues from Detective Conan. Bronze statues of the police officer Ryōtsu from Kochikame stand around Kameari in Tokyo.

Museums

The Osamu Tezuka Manga Museum in Takarazuka, the Fujiko F. Fujio Museum in Kawasaki and the Kyoto International Manga Museum are popular destinations. In Tokyo, the Tokiwa-sō Manga Museum recreates the apartment building where Tezuka and the young artists who followed him lived.

Visiting well

Remember that many locations are ordinary neighbourhoods, schools and homes. Be quiet, do not trespass, and follow local rules. Many towns welcome fans, but they also rely on visitors behaving respectfully.

Why it matters

Visiting these places shows how manga turns ordinary streets into memorable scenes, and how fans in turn have changed the towns that inspired them.

title: Manga in the 2020s
question: What is happening in manga right now?
summary: How web serialisation, anime and global readers have shaped the manga of the 2020s, and the series that defined the decade so far. 48 in the letters, reducing to 3.
body:
3Reduced, this question gives 3. It sits on The Telling with the rest of an act of telling.

A new landscape

The manga of the 2020s look different from those of a generation earlier, not because the stories changed most, but because of where and how people read them. Phones, apps and simultaneous translation have made manga a truly global medium.

The rise of the app

Publishers' apps moved to the centre of the industry. Shueisha's Shōnen Jump+ produced Spy × Family, Kaiju No. 8 and Dandadan, and the second part of Chainsaw Man moved there. A series can now become a major hit without appearing in a print magazine first.

Global readers

Official English chapters are now often released on the same day as in Japan, through services such as Shueisha's Manga Plus. Readers around the world discuss new chapters together, and international sales have become important to publishers.

The anime effect

Anime adaptations arrive quickly and spread worldwide through streaming. A strong adaptation can transform a manga's fortunes, as with Oshi no Ko, Bocchi the Rock! and Frieren.

Trends

Several trends stand out: adult heroes, as in Sakamoto Days and Kaiju No. 8; stories about creative work and the entertainment industry, as in Oshi no Ko and Blue Period; and reflective fantasy, as in Frieren, which looks back on an adventure after it has ended. Battle manga such as Jujutsu Kaisen and Chainsaw Man remain hugely popular.

Why it matters

Understanding these changes helps explain why some series spread so fast, and why the manga you hear about may have started on a phone. The fundamentals, though, are unchanged: weekly deadlines, editors, reader feedback and creators trying to tell a story that readers will come back for.

Artists drawing artists

Manga artists spend their lives on creative work, and many of the medium's best stories are about it. They show the training, the doubt, the competition and the moments when something finally works.

Making manga

Bakuman, by the creators of Death Note, follows two boys trying to become Weekly Shōnen Jump artists, with detailed scenes of editors, surveys and deadlines. Tatsuki Fujimoto's Look Back is a short, powerful story about two young artists and what drawing means to them. Yoshihiro Tatsumi's A Drifting Life is a memoir of the birth of gekiga.

Painting and art school

Blue Period follows a student preparing for Japan's most competitive art university, explaining real techniques and critiques. Honey and Clover follows art students facing love and their futures.

Music

Nodame Cantabile follows classical musicians from college to the concert stage. Nana follows a punk singer and the music business. Bocchi the Rock! and K-On! are comedies about amateur bands, the first about a guitarist overcoming crippling anxiety.

What they share

These stories treat creative work as work: it takes practice, involves failure and depends on others. They also show its rewards, the feeling of expressing something real, and why people keep going despite the odds.

Why read them

Manga about making art are often among the most personal works their creators produce, and they can inspire readers to start creating themselves.

title: Manga about war and the atomic bomb
question: How has manga told the story of the Second World War?
summary: How manga artists who lived through the war, and those who came after, have told its story, from Barefoot Gen to In This Corner of the World. Filed under 3, the telling.
body:
3Reduced, this question gives 3. It sits on The Telling with the rest of an act of telling.

Artists who were there

Many of the artists who built modern manga lived through the Second World War as children or soldiers. Osamu Tezuka was a teenager in Osaka during the air raids; Shigeru Mizuki fought on the island of New Britain and lost his left arm; Keiji Nakazawa was six when the atomic bomb fell on Hiroshima. Their experience shaped what they drew.

Barefoot Gen

Nakazawa's Barefoot Gen (1973–1987) is the most famous war manga. It tells the story of the bombing of Hiroshima and its aftermath through a boy whose family is destroyed, as Nakazawa's was. Its unflinching images of the bomb's effects have made it both a classic and a subject of controversy.

The soldier's view

Mizuki's Onward Towards Our Noble Deaths (1973) is based on his own unit, ordered to make a suicidal charge and condemned when some survived. He later drew a long history of the Shōwa era, mixing his own life with the nation's. Their tone is bitter, humane and sometimes darkly funny.

Tezuka

Tezuka returned to the war many times. Adolf (1983–1985) follows three men named Adolf, including Hitler, in a story of the Holocaust and Japan's alliance with Germany.

Later generations

Artists born long after the war have approached it differently. Fumiyo Kōno's Town of Evening Calm, Country of Cherry Blossoms (2003–2004) is about the long shadow of Hiroshima, and her In This Corner of the World (2007–2009) shows ordinary life in wartime Kure, adapted as an acclaimed film in 2016.

Why it matters

Manga have been one of the most powerful ways of remembering the war in Japan, especially for young readers, and their testimony has reached readers around the world.

title: Samurai and ninja manga
question: What are the best samurai and ninja manga?
summary: Samurai and ninja manga, from Lone Wolf and Cub and Kamui Den to Vagabond, Blade of the Immortal, Rurouni Kenshin, Gintama and Naruto: realism, legend, comedy and fantasy in Japan's period drama. 77 in the letters, reducing to 5.
body:
5Question sums to 77 and reduces to 5 — The Turn, where the reference files a turn.

Period drama

Samurai and ninja stories belong to jidaigeki, period drama set in Japan's past, a genre shared with film and television. In manga it ranges from grim realism to legend, comedy and fantasy, and it carries some of the medium's greatest artwork.

The gekiga classics

Kazuo Koike and Goseki Kojima's Lone Wolf and Cub (1970–1976) follows Ogami Ittō, the shogun's executioner, who is framed and disgraced and becomes an assassin for hire, wandering Edo-period Japan with his infant son in a wooden cart. Its stark, cinematic episodes, full of silent pages, made it one of the most influential manga abroad; American comics and films have borrowed from it openly. Sanpei Shirato's Kamui Den (1964–1971), serialised in the alternative magazine Garo, follows a ninja born an outcast, and uses him to tell a history of class: of peasants, samurai and the people beneath both.

The great swordsman

Takehiko Inoue's Vagabond (1998–), based on Eiji Yoshikawa's novel Musashi, retells the life of Miyamoto Musashi, Japan's most famous swordsman, from violent youth towards an understanding of what the sword is for. Its brushwork is among the most admired in manga. It has been on hiatus since 2015. Hiroaki Samura's Blade of the Immortal (1993–2012) follows Manji, a samurai who cannot die, protecting a girl seeking revenge for her parents, and asks what revenge costs.

The end of the samurai

Nobuhiro Watsuki's Rurouni Kenshin (1994–1999) is set in the Meiji era, after the samurai class has been abolished. Kenshin, once a legendary assassin, wanders with a reverse-blade sword and a vow never to kill again, and the past keeps coming for him. It is a battle shōnen with real historical weight, and its live-action films were hits. Hideaki Sorachi's Gintama (2003–2019) parodies the whole genre: aliens have conquered Edo, swords are banned, and a lazy ex-samurai does odd jobs.

Ninja

Historical ninja were spies and saboteurs, and Shirato drew them realistically. Most later manga made them fantasy. Masashi Kishimoto's Naruto imagines whole villages of ninja with supernatural techniques, and became one of the best-selling manga ever. Osamu Tezuka's Dororo mixes a swordsman's quest with demons.

Other periods

Satoru Noda's Golden Kamuy is set just after the samurai age, in Hokkaido after the Russo-Japanese War, and one of its characters is a famous swordsman of the shogunate's last defenders who survived far longer than history allows. Kōta Hirano's Drifters drops a samurai of Sekigahara into a fantasy world.

Where to start

For adventure, start with Rurouni Kenshin. For art and depth, Vagabond or Lone Wolf and Cub. For action with a supernatural twist, Blade of the Immortal. For comedy, Gintama. For fantasy ninja, Naruto.

title: LGBTQ+ stories in manga
question: Are there manga about LGBTQ+ characters and experiences?
summary: From the shōnen-ai of the 1970s to manga about transgender youth, gay families and queer memoir, how manga has told LGBTQ+ stories. Read from the care, as a 6.
body:
6Filed under 6. The Care takes an obligation, and this explainer is holds one.

A long history

Manga has told stories of same-sex love and gender for decades. In the 1970s, women artists of the Year 24 Group created shōnen-ai, stories of love between boys written for girls, in works such as Moto Hagio's The Heart of Thomas. Riyoko Ikeda's The Rose of Versailles made a woman raised as a man its hero.

Boys' love and yuri

Shōnen-ai grew into boys' love, or BL, a large genre written mostly by and for women. Yuri, stories of love between women, developed in parallel. Both are genres with their own conventions, and they do not always reflect the lives of real LGBTQ+ people, but they have been important to many readers.

Trans stories

Takako Shimura's Wandering Son (2002–2013) follows two transgender children through puberty with honesty and tenderness. Yuhki Kamatani's Our Dreams at Dusk follows a gay teenager who finds a community of LGBTQ+ people.

Families and society

Gengoroh Tagame's My Brother's Husband (2014–2017), published in a mainstream magazine, follows a father learning to accept his late twin brother's Canadian husband. It was written to explain gay life to a general audience and won wide attention.

Memoir

Kabi Nagata's My Lesbian Experience with Loneliness (2016), an essay manga about sexuality, depression and family, found a large audience abroad and showed how personal manga could speak to readers' own experience.

Why it matters

These works show the range of LGBTQ+ stories in manga, from genre romance to realism and memoir, and how they have changed over time.

title: Romantic comedy in manga
question: What are the best romantic comedy manga?
summary: Romantic comedy in manga, from Urusei Yatsura, Maison Ikkoku and Kimagure Orange Road to Kaguya-sama, The Quintessential Quintuplets and Fly Me to the Moon: how the genre works, its main types and where to start. 100 in the letters, reducing to 1.
body:
1Reduced, this question gives 1. It sits on The Opening with the rest of a first move.

The engine

Romantic comedy is one of manga's biggest genres, in shōnen, shōjo, seinen and josei magazines alike. Its engine is a feeling that cannot be spoken: two people who obviously like each other, and everything that stops them saying so, from pride and shyness to misunderstandings, rivals, families and bad timing. In a serial that can run for years, the confession is usually the ending, so everything is built around the delay.

The classics

Rumiko Takahashi shaped the modern genre. Urusei Yatsura (1978–1987) is chaotic slapstick about an alien princess and the lecherous boy she claims, which slowly reveals a real love story underneath. Maison Ikkoku (1980–1987) follows a hapless student and the young widow who manages his boarding house through years of near-misses, and lets its characters grow up. Ranma ½ adds martial arts and a curse that turns its hero into a girl. Izumi Matsumoto's Kimagure Orange Road (1984–1987) built a love triangle around a boy with psychic powers, and Kōsuke Fujishima's Ah! My Goddess began when a college student dialled a wrong number and reached a goddess.

The battle of wills

Aka Akasaka's Kaguya-sama: Love Is War (2015–2022) turned the genre into strategy. Kaguya and Miyuki, the two geniuses of their school's student council, are each too proud to confess first, so they scheme to make the other admit it. The comedy comes from how clever both are, and the series grows into a warm story about a whole council of friends. Sōichirō Yamamoto's Teasing Master Takagi-san distils the same idea into a middle-school girl who always wins and a boy who never notices why.

Harem and multiple choice

In a harem rom-com, one lead is surrounded by several love interests, and the question of who will be chosen runs the series. Ken Akamatsu's Love Hina (1998–2001) put a hapless student in charge of a girls' dormitory. Negi Haruba's The Quintessential Quintuplets (2017–2020) gave the format a mystery: its first chapter shows the hero's wedding to one of five identical sisters he tutors, without saying which.

After the confession

Some series skip the delay. In Kenjirō Hata's Fly Me to the Moon, the leads marry in the first volume, and the comedy is about learning to live together.

Adult romance

Fujita's Wotakoi follows two otaku office workers who start dating and try to hide their hobbies at work. Tomoko Ninomiya's Nodame Cantabile pairs a perfectionist music student with a brilliant, chaotic pianist. The tropes are the same, but the obstacles are jobs and adulthood. Our guide to the dere types explains the fan vocabulary for rom-com characters.

Where to start

Start with Kaguya-sama for a modern classic, Maison Ikkoku for a story that takes its time, Takagi-san for something short and sweet, and Wotakoi for romance between adults.

title: Manga about food and cooking
question: What are the best manga about food?
summary: Food and cooking manga, from Oishinbo and Cooking Papa to Food Wars!, What Did You Eat Yesterday?, Sweetness & Lightning, The Solitary Gourmet and Delicious in Dungeon: the main kinds and where to start. 102 in the letters, reducing to 3.
body:
3The letters of this question total 102, a 3 — the number of communication, creativity, and the public stage.

A huge genre

Food manga are one of the medium's largest genres, and they come in every shape: dramatic contests, careful domestic stories, travelogues, histories and fantasy. Many include real recipes, and some are as much about Japanese food culture as about their characters. The glossary entry on cooking manga traces the genre's terms.

The gourmet classic

Oishinbo, written by Tetsu Kariya and drawn by Akira Hanasaki, has run in Big Comic Spirits since 1983, with more than a hundred volumes, and has been on hiatus since 2014. Its hero, a cynical newspaper journalist, is assigned to compile the "ultimate menu" while feuding with his father, a gourmet artist who runs a rival project. Every chapter is an argument about ingredients, technique and taste, and it shaped how Japan talked about food for decades.

Cooking as battle

Yūto Tsukuda and Shun Saeki's Food Wars! (2012–2019) turns cooking into battle manga: students at an elite culinary academy settle disputes with cooking duels. The dishes were developed with a professional chef, and the tasters' reactions are famously outrageous. It descends from earlier cooking-contest manga such as Mister Ajikko, which made young chefs into rivals in the 1980s.

Cooking as care

Gido Amagakure's Sweetness & Lightning (2013–2018) follows a widowed teacher who cannot cook learning to make proper meals for his young daughter, with the help of a student whose mother runs a restaurant. Fumi Yoshinaga's What Did You Eat Yesterday? (2007–) follows a lawyer who cooks dinner every night for his partner; each chapter is a realistic recipe, sized for two and costed. Tochi Ueyama's Cooking Papa, running in Morning since 1985, follows a salaryman who secretly cooks everything for his family.

Eating alone

Masayuki Kusumi and Jirō Taniguchi's The Solitary Gourmet follows a salesman who eats alone at ordinary restaurants between appointments and narrates his thoughts about every dish. Almost nothing happens, which is the point. It became a long-running television drama and a model for quiet food stories.

Food in fantasy and farming

Ryoko Kui's Delicious in Dungeon (2014–2023) follows adventurers who cook and eat the monsters of a dungeon to survive, with the ecology and recipes worked out in loving detail; it grows into a serious fantasy. Hiromu Arakawa's Silver Spoon shows where food comes from, at an agricultural high school in Hokkaido.

Where to start

Try Food Wars! for excitement, Sweetness & Lightning or What Did You Eat Yesterday? for comfort, Delicious in Dungeon for fantasy, and Silver Spoon for the farm behind the plate.

title: How manga reach the stage and screen
question: Why are so many manga adapted into films, dramas and musicals?
summary: How manga become anime, live-action films and dramas, 2.5D stage musicals and international productions: why adaptation is so common, how it is organised, and what makes some adaptations work. Read from the care, as a 6.
body:
6A 6 by its question: nurturer & harmonizer, and therefore the care.

Many lives

A successful manga rarely stays on the page. It may become an anime, a live-action film or television drama, a stage musical, a video game and, increasingly, an international production. In Japan this is planned as a media mix, with each form advertising the others and reaching a different audience.

How adaptations are organised

Most Japanese adaptations are financed by a production committee: a group of companies, typically the publisher, a broadcaster or streamer, a music label, merchandise makers and the studio, who share the cost and the profit. The publisher's interest is the manga. An adaptation is, among other things, an advertisement for the books.

Anime

Anime is the most common adaptation and often the most important. A good one can multiply a manga's readership, especially abroad; Demon Slayer's sales rose dramatically after its 2019 anime, and its film Mugen Train became the highest-grossing film in Japanese history. Modern adaptations usually air in seasons, with breaks while the manga moves ahead, rather than running year-round with filler as they once did.

Live action in Japan

Japanese film and television have adapted manga for decades. Television dramas of Great Teacher Onizuka, Boys Over Flowers and Nodame Cantabile were national hits, and Boys Over Flowers was also remade in Taiwan and Korea. Films of Death Note, Rurouni Kenshin, Thermae Romae, Kingdom and Golden Kamuy brought manga to cinema audiences who might never read one. The glossary entry on live-action adaptation covers the debates they provoke.

The stage

Stage adaptations, called 2.5D, are a major industry. The Takarazuka Revue's The Rose of Versailles, first staged in 1974, showed what manga could do on stage. Musicals of Sailor Moon began in 1993, and The Prince of Tennis musical, from 2003, established the modern form, with young actors, elaborate staging and long national tours. Stage versions of Haikyu!! and Kuroko's Basketball play to large audiences.

International productions

Hollywood and streaming services have adapted manga with mixed results. Ghost in the Shell (2017) and Alita: Battle Angel (2019) were expensive productions with mixed receptions; Netflix's Death Note (2017) was poorly received, while its One Piece (2023) was welcomed by many fans. The most acclaimed foreign adaptation is probably Park Chan-wook's Korean film Oldboy (2003), based on a Japanese manga.

What makes an adaptation work

Successful adaptations tend to understand what made the original matter, its characters, tone and heart, rather than copying its look. Fans notice when an adaptation misses the point, and the most loved ones often change a great deal on the surface to keep what is underneath. Our guide to what changes in adaptation looks at the craft.

title: Short manga you can finish in a weekend
question: What are some great manga that are only a few volumes long?
summary: Complete manga you can finish in a weekend, from one-volume works like Look Back, Goodbye Eri, Domu and Sand Land to short series like Uzumaki, Planetes, A Silent Voice and Pluto, sorted by length. The question reduces to 9 — the closing.
body:
9A 9 by its question: humanitarian & sage, and therefore the closing.

Why read short manga

Many famous manga run for dozens of volumes, which can be daunting. But some of the best manga are short and complete, and they are the ideal way to try a new creator or genre, or to fill a single weekend. A tankōbon volume holds around 200 pages and takes an hour or two to read, so anything up to eight volumes fits in a weekend.

One volume

Tatsuki Fujimoto's Look Back (2021) follows two girls in rural Japan who draw manga, one confident and one who never leaves her room, across the years of their partnership. It is one of the most acclaimed one-shots of recent years and was made into a film. His Goodbye, Eri (2022) plays with film, memory and unreliable storytelling. Katsuhiro Otomo's Domu (1980–1981), a psychic duel between an old man and a little girl in a housing complex, was the rehearsal for Akira. Akira Toriyama's Sand Land (2000) is a light, charming desert adventure about a demon prince and an old sheriff in search of water. Masamune Shirow's Ghost in the Shell is a single dense volume.

Two or three volumes

Junji Ito's Uzumaki is a horror story about a town consumed by spirals, and his Gyo has fish walking out of the sea on mechanical legs. Inio Asano's Solanin follows young people in Tokyo unsure what to do with their lives. Taiyō Matsumoto's Tekkonkinkreet is about two orphan boys who rule the rooftops of a changing city. Jirō Taniguchi's A Distant Neighborhood sends a middle-aged man back to his fourteen-year-old self. Yoshihiro Togashi's Level E is a sharp science-fiction comedy about an alien prince on Earth.

Four to eight volumes

Makoto Yukimura's Planetes is hard science fiction about space-debris collectors, in four volumes. Go Nagai's Devilman is five, and its ending is famous. Mari Yamazaki's Thermae Romae is six volumes of time-slipping bath comedy. Yoshitoki Ōima's A Silent Voice, in seven, follows a boy who bullied a deaf classmate and tries, years later, to make amends. Naoki Urasawa's Pluto, in eight, retells a story from Astro Boy as a thriller. Katsuhiro Otomo's Akira is six large volumes, a big weekend but a complete one.

Classics in short pieces

Moto Hagio's They Were Eleven is a short shōjo science-fiction mystery. Osamu Tezuka's Black Jack is long, but every chapter is a complete story, so any volume can be read alone.

How to choose

If you like emotional drama, start with Look Back or A Silent Voice. For science fiction, Planetes or They Were Eleven. For horror, Uzumaki or Domu. For something light, Sand Land or Level E. Our list of twelve manga to start with has longer suggestions.

title: Science fiction in manga
question: What are the essential science fiction manga?
summary: Science fiction runs through manga from Astro Boy and Phoenix to Akira, Ghost in the Shell, Planetes and Land of the Lustrous: robots, cyborgs, space, ruined cities and what they say about being human, with where to start. Filed under 4, the structure.
body:
4The letters of this question total 103, a 4 — the number of structure, labour, and the building of lasting systems.

From the beginning

Science fiction is part of modern manga from its start. Osamu Tezuka's Astro Boy (1952–1968), about a robot boy built by a grieving scientist, asked whether a machine could have a soul, and the question has never left the medium. Tezuka's Phoenix moved between the distant past and the far future, treating science fiction as a way to think about life and death on the largest scale.

Heroes and machines

The 1960s and 1970s turned science fiction into adventure. Shōtarō Ishinomori's Cyborg 009 (1964) gathered nine people turned into cyborgs against their will. Go Nagai's Mazinger Z (1972) put a pilot inside a giant robot and founded the mecha genre. Leiji Matsumoto's Galaxy Express 999 (1977–1981) sent a boy across the galaxy on a space train in search of a free mechanical body, and found melancholy in every stop. The giant robot reached its most psychological form in the 1990s with Neon Genesis Evangelion.

Shōjo science fiction

In the 1970s, the women artists of the Year 24 Group brought science fiction into girls' manga. Moto Hagio's They Were Eleven (1975) sets ten cadets on a derelict ship for a survival exam, only to find there are eleven of them. It is a locked-room mystery, and also a story about gender: one cadet belongs to a species that chooses its sex at adulthood.

Cyberpunk

Katsuhiro Otomo's Akira (1982–1990) imagined Neo-Tokyo, rebuilt after a war, and a teenage biker gang caught up in government experiments on children with terrible powers. Its 1988 film changed how the world saw anime. Masamune Shirow's Ghost in the Shell (1989–1990) followed a cyborg agent in a networked future and asked what is left of a person when body and memory can both be replaced; its 1995 film influenced Hollywood science fiction for a decade.

Hard science fiction

Makoto Yukimura's Planetes (1999–2004) follows the crew who clear debris from orbit in the 2070s. It is careful about physics and about work, and its drama is about why people go to space at all. Tsutomu Nihei's BLAME! sends a silent wanderer through an endless megastructure, and his Knights of Sidonia follows the crew of a seed ship fighting shapeshifting aliens.

Strange futures

Haruko Ichikawa's Land of the Lustrous (2012–2024) is set in a far future where gem-bodied people fight moon-dwellers who want to break them into ornaments; it is beautiful, strange and increasingly philosophical. Naoki Urasawa's Pluto retells an Astro Boy story as a detective thriller about robot grief. Yoshihiro Togashi's Level E is comic science fiction about an alien prince who treats Earth as his playground.

Today

Riichirō Inagaki and Boichi's Dr. Stone (2017–2022) has humanity turned to stone for thousands of years and a teenage genius rebuilding civilisation one invention at a time. Inio Asano's Dead Dead Demon's Dededede Destruction (2014–2022) is about two schoolgirls living ordinary lives under an alien mothership hanging over Tokyo. The glossary entry on SF manga has more.

Where to start

For spectacle, start with Akira. For ideas, Ghost in the Shell. For realism, Planetes. For a short classic, They Were Eleven. For something new and strange, Land of the Lustrous.

title: Magic and wizards in manga
question: What are the best manga about magic, witches and wizards?
summary: From Frieren and Witch Hat Atelier to Black Clover, Fairy Tail, Magi and Fullmetal Alchemist: the ways manga imagines magic, as a craft to learn, a power to fight with or a burden to carry, and where to start reading. Read from the structure, as a 4.
body:
4Filed under 4. The Structure takes a structure, and this explainer is holds one.

Why magic

Magic is one of fantasy's oldest ideas, and manga has used it in almost every way possible: as a power to fight with, a craft to learn, a science with laws, a burden, or a source of wonder. How a series imagines its magic tells you a great deal about what kind of story it is. A magic system with strict rules supports puzzles and strategy; magic that is mysterious supports wonder and dread.

Magic as a craft

Kamome Shirahama's Witch Hat Atelier (2016–) imagines magic as drawing: spells are glyphs inked with special pens, and anyone with the right tools could cast them. That is why the witches keep it secret, and why the series' heroine, Coco, an ordinary girl who sees a witch at work, becomes dangerous by learning. The art, detailed like book illustration, makes every spell look like something you could copy. Kanehito Yamada and Tsukasa Abe's Frieren: Beyond Journey's End (2020–) treats magic as a lifetime's study. Its elf heroine has spent a thousand years collecting spells, there are mage schools and examinations, and magic has a history: a demon's killing spell, studied and countered, becomes everyday offensive magic within a human lifetime.

Magic as power

Battle manga turn magic into a power system. In Yūki Tabata's Black Clover (2015–2026), everyone in the kingdom receives a grimoire and has magic except Asta, who wants to become the Wizard King and fights with an anti-magic sword. Hiro Mashima's Fairy Tail (2006–2017) follows a guild of rowdy wizards who take jobs, fight dark guilds and value friendship above everything. Shinobu Ohtaka's Magi (2009–2017) draws on the Arabian Nights, with dungeons, djinn and a boy who turns out to be a rare magician who can draw power from the world itself. Ken Akamatsu's Negima! begins as a comedy about a ten-year-old wizard teaching at a girls' school and turns into a full magical battle manga.

Magic as science

Hiromu Arakawa's Fullmetal Alchemist (2001–2010) presents alchemy as a discipline with laws. Its first principle, equivalent exchange, says you cannot create something from nothing, and the story begins with two brothers who break it trying to bring their mother back. The rules make the fights into puzzles and the moral stakes clear.

Magical girls

A whole genre turns on magic. Naoko Takeuchi's Sailor Moon and CLAMP's Cardcaptor Sakura are the classics of the magical girl, where magic arrives with a transformation, a mascot and a duty.

Darker magic

Magic can be cruel. In Q Hayashida's Dorohedoro (2000–2018), sorcerers release magic as smoke from their fingertips and use the people of a grim city as test subjects for fun; the hero is a man whose head was turned into a lizard's. In Kazue Katō's Blue Exorcist, magic is a weapon in a war against demons, and the hero is the son of Satan training to fight his own father.

Where to start

For wonder, start with Witch Hat Atelier. For quiet reflection, Frieren. For action, Black Clover or Fairy Tail. For rules and puzzles, Fullmetal Alchemist. For a classic, Cardcaptor Sakura.

title: Manga set in history outside Japan
question: Are there manga about history in other countries?
summary: Manga set in the history of other countries, from The Rose of Versailles and Vinland Saga to Kingdom, Emma, A Bride's Story and Historie: what they cover, how accurate they are and where to start. The question reduces to 1 — the opening.
body:
1One — initiative. That is the reduction of this question, and the shelf it is read from.

Looking abroad

Japanese history fills a great many manga, but creators have also told stories set all over the world, and several of them became classics. Manga is well suited to history: it can show clothes, buildings, tools and daily life in a detail that prose must describe, and long serials can follow characters across decades of events.

Europe

Riyoko Ikeda's The Rose of Versailles (1972–1973) is set in France before and during the Revolution. Its heroine, Oscar, is raised as a man to command the royal guard, and the story moves from Marie Antoinette's court to the storming of the Bastille. It became a phenomenon in Japan and a long-running Takarazuka musical. Makoto Yukimura's Vinland Saga (2005–2025) follows Thorfinn, a young Icelander, through the Danish wars for England in the early eleventh century, and then through what comes after violence. Kaoru Mori's Emma (2002–2008) is a romance across classes in 1890s London. Fuyumi Soryo's Cesare follows Cesare Borgia as a student in Renaissance Italy.

The ancient world

Hitoshi Iwaaki's Historie (2003–) follows Eumenes of Cardia, a Greek who became Alexander the Great's secretary, from a childhood full of surprises. Mari Yamazaki's Thermae Romae plays Rome for comedy, sending a bath architect forward to modern Japan.

Asia

Yasuhisa Hara's Kingdom (2006–) dramatises the wars of China's Warring States period, following a war orphan who wants to become a great general and the young king who will unify China as its first emperor. It is long, epic and very popular. Osamu Tezuka's Buddha retells the life of Siddhartha in ancient India. Kaoru Mori's A Bride's Story (2008–) is set among the peoples of nineteenth-century Central Asia, beginning with a young woman married to a boy eight years her junior.

The twentieth century

Tezuka's Message to Adolf follows three men named Adolf through the Second World War in Germany and Japan. Naoki Urasawa's Monster and Billy Bat use twentieth-century European and American history as the background to their thrillers.

History made fantasy

Some works borrow history for invented worlds. Hiromu Arakawa's The Heroic Legend of Arslan is set in a kingdom inspired by ancient Persia, and her Fullmetal Alchemist draws on early twentieth-century Europe. Kōta Hirano's Drifters pulls real historical figures, from a samurai of Sekigahara to Joan of Arc, into a fantasy war.

How accurate are they?

It varies. Kaoru Mori is known for meticulous research into costume, crafts and households, and Yukimura for the texture of Viking life. Kingdom uses real events and generals but invents most of what it shows, because the sources are sparse. Treat these as historical fiction: often well researched, always dramatised.

Where to start

For romance and politics, start with The Rose of Versailles. For war and its consequences, Vinland Saga. For daily life, A Bride's Story or Emma. For battles on a vast scale, Kingdom.

title: Time travel in manga
question: What are the best manga about time travel?
summary: Time travel in manga, from Doraemon and The Drifting Classroom to Erased, Tokyo Revengers, JIN and A Distant Neighborhood: the kinds of time-travel story manga tells, and where to start. The question reduces to 4 — the structure.
body:
4A 4 by its question: builder & organizer, and therefore the structure.

Why time travel

Time travel lets a story ask a simple question: what would you change if you could go back? Manga has answered it in thrillers, romances, comedies and horror, and Japanese fiction has its own long tradition of the time slip, popularised by Yasutaka Tsutsui's novel The Girl Who Leapt Through Time in the 1960s.

Going back to save someone

The most common form sends an adult back to their youth to prevent a tragedy. Kei Sanbe's Erased (2012–2016) follows Satoru, a struggling manga artist with a strange ability to jump a few minutes back in time, who is suddenly thrown back eighteen years to his childhood, weeks before a classmate was murdered. Ken Wakui's Tokyo Revengers (2017–2022) sends a 26-year-old back to his delinquent school days to save the girlfriend he lost, and each return to the present shows what his changes broke. Ichigo Takano's Orange reverses the direction: a girl receives letters from her future self, asking her to save a classmate.

Going back to remember

Jirō Taniguchi's A Distant Neighborhood is gentler. A man of forty-eight wakes in his fourteen-year-old body in the 1960s, months before his father left the family without explanation, and relives the summer with adult eyes. It is less about changing the past than understanding it.

Time slips into history

Rumiko Takahashi's Inuyasha sends a schoolgirl down a well into Japan's warring-states period, and her Mao sends a girl into the Taishō era. Motoka Murakami's JIN drops a modern neurosurgeon into the 1860s, where he has to practise medicine without antibiotics or anaesthetic and finds himself changing history. Kaiji Kawaguchi's Zipang sends a modern Japanese destroyer back to 1942, in the middle of the Pacific War. Mari Yamazaki's Thermae Romae runs the other way: an ancient Roman bath architect keeps slipping into modern Japanese bathhouses and takes the ideas home.

Comedy and horror

Fujiko F. Fujio's Doraemon is a robot cat from the twenty-second century sent back to help a hopeless boy, and his time machine sits in a drawer of Nobita's desk. In Kazuo Umezu's The Drifting Classroom (1972–1974), a whole elementary school is thrown into a ruined future wasteland, and the children have to survive without adults. It is one of the most frightening manga ever drawn.

Loops

A related form traps the hero in a loop, reliving the same stretch of time until they get it right. It is common in light novels and their manga, where the reset works like a game's continue screen, and it often turns into a story about trauma, since the hero remembers every failure.

For a thriller, start with Erased. For action, Tokyo Revengers. For history and medicine, JIN. For something quiet, A Distant Neighborhood. For laughs, Thermae Romae. For horror, The Drifting Classroom.

title: Manga about grown-ups
question: Are there manga about adults instead of teenagers?
summary: Manga about work, money, couples, parenthood and growing old, from What Did You Eat Yesterday? and Usagi Drop to Kaiji, Inuyashiki and Our Little Sister, and the magazines that publish them. Filed under 3, the telling.
body:
3The letters of this question total 75, a 3 — the number of communication, creativity, and the public stage.

Not just for teenagers

The manga best known abroad mostly star teenagers, because they come from shōnen and shōjo magazines. But Japan also publishes seinen magazines for adult men and josei magazines for adult women, and their stories are about grown-up lives: jobs, marriages, children, debts, ageing parents and the feeling that time is passing. If you have aged out of school stories, there is a whole shelf written for you.

Couples and daily life

Fumi Yoshinaga's What Did You Eat Yesterday? (2007–), in Morning, follows Shiro, a careful lawyer, and Kenji, a cheerful hairdresser, a gay couple in middle age. Every chapter ends with Shiro cooking dinner, with the recipe on the page, and around the food the series deals with coming out to parents, money, illness and getting older together. The characters age in real time, which is rare and quietly moving. Fujita's Wotakoi: Love Is Hard for Otaku (2014–2021) is lighter: two colleagues, childhood acquaintances, start dating and try to keep their gaming and fan habits from their office.

Parenthood

Yumi Unita's Usagi Drop (2005–2011), in Feel Young, begins at a funeral, where Daikichi, a single man of thirty, learns that his grandfather left behind a six-year-old daughter nobody wants, and takes her home. The first half, about a man rearranging his life around a child, is one of the best stories about parenting in manga; the second half, which jumps ten years ahead, divides readers. Akimi Yoshida's Our Little Sister (2006–2018) follows three adult sisters in Kamakura who take in the teenage half-sister they met at their father's funeral. Tatsuya Endo's Spy x Family plays family for comedy: a spy, an assassin and a telepathic child pretend to be a household, and find that they are one.

Work and money

Kenshi Hirokane's Section Chief Kōsaku Shima has followed one salaryman's career, through promotions and affairs, since 1983. Tetsu Kariya and Akira Hanasaki's Oishinbo follows a cynical newspaper journalist assigned to create the ultimate menu, and turns every chapter into an argument about food. Nobuyuki Fukumoto's Kaiji is about a man in his twenties with no job and a friend's debt to pay, who is drawn into a series of lethal gambling games; it is as much about poverty as about games. Inio Asano's Solanin follows a young office worker who quits her job and has to decide what her life is for. The glossary entry on work manga covers the wider genre.

Getting older

Hiroya Oku's Inuyashiki (2014–2017) starts with a 58-year-old man whose family ignores him and whose doctor has just given him months to live. Then he is killed and rebuilt as a machine, and must decide what to do with power at the end of a life nobody valued. Jirō Taniguchi's A Distant Neighborhood sends a 48-year-old man back into his fourteen-year-old body, months before his father left the family, and asks what he would change. Yoshihiro Tatsumi's A Drifting Life is an autobiography of a manga artist's youth, told from the far end of a career.

Where to find them

In Japan, these stories run in magazines such as Morning, Big Comic Original, Feel Young and Flowers. In English, look for the seinen and josei labels, or for publishers' literary lines. Our explainer on shōnen, seinen, shōjo and josei explains how the labels work.

Where to start

For warmth, start with What Did You Eat Yesterday? or Usagi Drop. For comedy, Wotakoi or Spy x Family. For something darker, Kaiji or Inuyashiki. For a short, literary read, A Distant Neighborhood.
