faq.answer: No. Japan's seinen and josei magazines, written for adult men and women, publish a great many stories about adults: their jobs, marriages, children, money and ageing. The teenage heroes most people know come from the shōnen and shōjo magazines.

faq.question: What is a good manga about an adult couple?
faq.answer: What Did You Eat Yesterday? follows a gay couple in their forties and fifties through years of home-cooked dinners, and the characters age in real time. Wotakoi is a lighter comedy about two office workers who are also otaku.

faq.answer: Usagi Drop, about a single man in his thirties who takes in a six-year-old girl, is the best known. Spy x Family is a comedy about a fake family that slowly becomes a real one.

faq.question: Is there a manga with an old hero?
faq.answer: Inuyashiki's hero is a 58-year-old man whom nobody respects, until he is rebuilt as a machine. Frieren's elf heroine is over a thousand years old, and the series is about what time means to her.

faq.question: What is a manga about work?
faq.answer: Section Chief Kōsaku Shima has followed one man's career through a Japanese company since 1983. Oishinbo follows a food journalist, and Kaiji is about what debt does to a man with no prospects.

question: Which Rumiko Takahashi manga should I read first?
summary: Start with Ranma ½ for comedy, Maison Ikkoku for romance, Inuyasha for adventure or Mao for something darker: a guide to Rumiko Takahashi's series, what each is like, and how long each one runs. 145 in the letters, reducing to 1.
body:
1The letters of this question total 145, a 1 — the number of beginnings, leadership, and the will to act alone.

Why Takahashi

Rumiko Takahashi has been producing hits since she was a university student in the late 1970s, almost all of them for Shogakukan's Weekly Shōnen Sunday. Her series are long, warm, funny and built on a simple engine: a group of stubborn people who cannot stop getting in each other's way. She has won the Shogakukan Manga Award twice, was inducted into the Eisner Hall of Fame in 2018 and received the Grand Prix at Angoulême in 2019. If you have read one of her series, you will recognise her in the others; if you have read none, there is a right starting point for almost any taste.

Ranma ½: start here for comedy

Ranma ½ (1987–1996, 38 volumes) is a martial-arts farce about a teenage boy who turns into a girl when splashed with cold water, and back again with hot. He is engaged to Akane, the daughter of a rival school, and the series fills up with rivals, suitors and fighters with absurd techniques. It is the easiest of her works to start: chapters are short, the jokes land immediately, and the cast grows one memorable lunatic at a time. A new anime adaptation in 2024 brought it to another generation.

Maison Ikkoku: start here for romance

Maison Ikkoku (1980–1987, 15 volumes) ran in Big Comic Spirits, a magazine for adult readers, and it shows. Godai, a hapless student who keeps failing his exams, falls for Kyoko, the young widow who manages his run-down boarding house. The neighbours are a nightmare, the misunderstandings pile up, and time passes for real: Godai has to find work, Kyoko has to decide whether she can love again. Many readers consider it her best work because it lets its characters grow up, and at 15 volumes it is her shortest long series.

Inuyasha: start here for adventure

Inuyasha (1996–2008, 56 volumes) sends Kagome, a modern schoolgirl, down a well into Japan's warring-states period, where she frees a half-demon and the two hunt the shards of a shattered jewel. It mixes yōkai battles, a slow-burn romance and a villain who holds the whole story together. It is long, but it moves, and its anime made it the gateway to manga for a great many readers outside Japan.

Urusei Yatsura: where it all began

Urusei Yatsura (1978–1987, 34 volumes) is the series that made her name. Ataru, a lecherous schoolboy, accidentally becomes engaged to Lum, an alien princess in a tiger-striped bikini who zaps him with electricity whenever he strays. It is chaotic, episodic and full of gods, aliens and monsters, and it set the pattern for the anarchic romantic comedy that later manga borrowed again and again. Its 2022 anime is an easy way in.

Rin-ne and Mao: the later series

Rin-ne (2009–2017, 40 volumes) is a gentle comedy about a girl who can see ghosts and a broke boy who guides them to the afterlife. Mao (2019–) is her darkest series: a girl who survived a strange accident walks into the Taishō era and meets an exorcist under a curse. It is a mystery more than a comedy, and the best choice if you want her storytelling without the slapstick.

The short stories

Takahashi also writes short. The Mermaid Saga, about people who eat mermaid flesh in search of immortality, is closer to horror than anything in her long series. The Rumic Theater stories, written for adult readers, are about ordinary middle-aged people in quiet trouble. Either is a good way to try her in an evening.

Where to start

For laughs, start with Ranma ½. For romance, Maison Ikkoku. For a long adventure, Inuyasha. For something darker, Mao or the Mermaid Saga. There is no shared continuity between her series, so you can go from any one to any other.

faq.answer: Ranma ½ is the easiest start: funny from the first chapter and made of short episodes. If you prefer romance, start with Maison Ikkoku; for a long adventure, Inuyasha; for a darker mystery, Mao.

faq.question: Which Rumiko Takahashi manga is the best?
faq.answer: Many readers name Maison Ikkoku, her romance for adult readers, because it is the one where her characters grow up. Inuyasha and Ranma ½ are her most popular.

faq.answer: No. Her series are separate stories with no shared continuity, so any of them can be read first. Reading them in publication order shows how her comedy turned into longer romance and adventure, but it is not required.

faq.question: Does Rumiko Takahashi still draw manga?
faq.answer: Yes. Mao has been running in Weekly Shōnen Sunday since 2019.

title: Where to start with CLAMP
question: Which CLAMP manga should I read first?
summary: Start with Cardcaptor Sakura for warmth, Magic Knight Rayearth for a short adventure, or Chobits and xxxHolic for older readers: a guide to CLAMP's series and the order to read the connected ones in. Read from the inquiry, as a 7.
body:
7Seven — inquiry. That is the reduction of this question, and the shelf it is read from.

Who CLAMP are

CLAMP is a team of four women, Nanase Ohkawa, Mokona, Tsubaki Nekoi and Satsuki Igarashi, who began as a larger doujinshi circle in Osaka in the 1980s and turned professional in 1989. Ohkawa usually leads on story and Mokona on the finished art, with the others sharing design and drawing, but the credit is always collective. They have worked for shōjo, shōnen and seinen magazines, which is unusual, and their work is recognisable in any of them: long-limbed elegant figures, lavish costumes and stories about fate, wishes and what getting what you want costs.

Cardcaptor Sakura: the warm start

Cardcaptor Sakura (1996–2000, 12 volumes) ran in Nakayoshi, a magazine for young girls. Sakura, a ten-year-old, accidentally releases a set of magical cards and has to capture them again, with her best friend filming every outfit. It is one of the best-loved magical-girl manga, and gentler and more generous than its premise suggests: it treats every kind of love with the same tenderness. A sequel, Clear Card, ran from 2016 to 2023.

Magic Knight Rayearth: the short adventure

Magic Knight Rayearth (1993–1996, 6 volumes) also ran in Nakayoshi. Three schoolgirls on a field trip to Tokyo Tower are pulled into another world to save its princess, become knights and pilot giant guardian beasts. It looks like a cheerful fantasy quest, and then the second half asks what the quest was really for. At six volumes, it is the quickest way to see what CLAMP do with a familiar formula.

Chobits and xxxHolic: for older readers

Chobits (2000–2002, 8 volumes) ran in Young Magazine. A struggling student finds a humanlike computer in the trash, and a fan-service comedy turns, slowly, into a serious story about what it means to love something that may not be able to love back. xxxHolic (2003–2011, 19 volumes) follows Watanuki, a boy plagued by spirits, who works for a witch who grants wishes at a price. It is episodic at first, a sequence of eerie, beautifully designed short stories, and becomes something sadder.

Tsubasa: the crossover

Tsubasa: Reservoir Chronicle (2003–2009, 28 volumes) ran in Weekly Shōnen Magazine. A boy named Syaoran travels between worlds to recover the memories of Princess Sakura, and every world is populated by characters from other CLAMP series, reimagined. It began the same year as xxxHolic, the two share the wish-granting witch, and they explain each other: the best way to read them is side by side.

X and the earlier work

X (1992–, 18 volumes) is CLAMP's apocalypse, a battle over the fate of Tokyo between two groups of people with supernatural powers. Its art is some of their most striking, but it has been on hiatus since 2003 and has no ending. Tokyo Babylon, which came before it, is a shorter, complete story with some of the same characters. Their professional debut, RG Veda, is a mythological epic in the style of their doujinshi years.

Where to start

For warmth, start with Cardcaptor Sakura. For a short adventure, Magic Knight Rayearth. For something adult and complete, Chobits. If you like either Tsubasa or xxxHolic, read them together. Save X for when you already love CLAMP and can live without an ending.

faq.answer: Side by side. Both began in 2003 and their stories cross repeatedly, so the clearest way is to alternate between them, roughly volume for volume. Each can be read alone, but some turns in one are explained in the other.

title: Where to start with Mitsuru Adachi
question: Which Mitsuru Adachi manga should I read first?
summary: Start with Cross Game for a complete story in 17 volumes, Touch for the classic or H2 for the most baseball: a guide to Mitsuru Adachi's quiet sports romances and what makes his storytelling different. Filed under 1, the opening.
body:
1Question sums to 136 and reduces to 1 — The Opening, where the reference files a first move.

Why Adachi

Mitsuru Adachi has been drawing manga for more than fifty years, most of them for Shogakukan's Weekly Shōnen Sunday, and he is one of the best-selling manga creators in Japan. His subject is nearly always the same: teenagers, high-school baseball, and love that nobody quite admits to. What makes him worth reading is not the subject but the way he tells it. If you have only read battle manga, Adachi will feel like a different medium.

The style: what he leaves out

Adachi's characters rarely say what they feel. When something important happens, he cuts away: to an empty sky, a quiet street, a cicada on a telegraph pole, a panel with no words at all. Jokes arrive exactly when a scene threatens to get sentimental. The art is clean and simple, and his leads look alike from one series to the next, which he turns into a running gag. The effect is that readers do the feeling themselves, and moments of grief or confession hit harder for being underplayed. His use of silence and pacing is studied by other artists; our guide to how manga controls pacing explains why it works.

Touch: the classic

Touch (1981–1986, 26 volumes) follows twin brothers, Tatsuya and Kazuya, and Minami, the girl next door. Kazuya is the hard-working star pitcher everyone expects to take Minami to Kōshien; Tatsuya is the lazy one. Then something happens that changes the story completely, and Tatsuya has to decide whether to take his brother's place. Touch was a national phenomenon in Japan, and it remains the series people mean when they say Adachi.

H2: the most baseball

H2 (1992–1999, 34 volumes) is his longest series. Hiro, a pitcher whose doctor said his elbow was finished, and Hideo, his best friend and the best slugger in the prefecture, end up on rival teams, with two girls between them. It is a love triangle that becomes a square, and the series builds patiently towards the moment Hiro and Hideo have to face each other at the plate. If you want baseball games told with real tension, start here.

Cross Game: the masterpiece

Cross Game (2005–2010, 17 volumes) opens with the childhood of Ko and Wakaba, who everyone assumes will grow up together. The first volume ends in a loss, and the rest of the series follows Ko through high school with Wakaba's younger sister, Aoba, a better pitcher than any boy on the team and furious that she cannot play in the official tournament. It is shorter, sadder and tighter than his earlier work, and many readers consider it his best.

The rest

Adachi has written about boxing (Katsu!), swimming (Rough) and more baseball than anyone. Miyuki, a romantic comedy, shared the Shogakukan Manga Award with Touch. Mix, which began in 2012, is set at the same school as Touch a generation later.

Where to start

Start with Cross Game if you want a complete story at a manageable length. Start with Touch for the classic, and H2 for the most baseball. Read one chapter slowly, and notice what he chooses not to show.

faq.answer: No. The games matter and are well told, but his series are mostly about friendship, love and grief, and the baseball is how those feelings get expressed.

faq.answer: Not in story, but they share types of characters, settings and jokes. Mix, which began in 2012, is set at the same school as Touch decades later, and Adachi often appears in his own pages to complain about deadlines.

faq.answer: It is deliberate and a running joke: his leads share faces from series to series, and the characters sometimes remark on it. The difference is in how they behave, not how they look.

title: Where to start with Naoki Urasawa
question: Which Naoki Urasawa manga should I read first?
summary: Start with Pluto for a complete thriller in 8 volumes, Monster for his classic or Yawara! for comedy: a guide to Naoki Urasawa's thrillers and sports stories, with how long each runs and what connects them. The question reduces to 6 — the care.
body:
6A 6 by its question: nurturer & harmonizer, and therefore the care.

Why Urasawa

Naoki Urasawa is one of the great storytellers of modern manga. His long thrillers follow mysteries across decades and countries, through large casts of ordinary people, and they are built to be impossible to put down. Each chapter ends on a question; each new character seems minor until they are given a whole chapter of their own life. His art is realistic and expressive, and his faces in particular, frightened, guilty, grieving, are what readers remember. Monster and Pluto both won the Grand Prize of the Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize.

Monster: the classic

Monster (1994–2001, 18 volumes) ran in Big Comic Original. Kenzo Tenma, a Japanese surgeon in Düsseldorf, chooses to operate on a shot boy instead of the mayor his hospital wants saved. Years later he learns that the boy has grown into a serial killer, and he crosses Germany and the Czech Republic to stop what he made possible. It is a manhunt, a mystery and a long argument about whether every life is worth saving.

20th Century Boys: the epic

20th Century Boys (1999–2006, 22 volumes) ran in Big Comic Spirits. Kenji, a convenience-store owner who once dreamed of rock stardom, realises that a cult threatening the world is enacting the apocalypse he and his friends invented as children in 1969. The story moves between the 1960s, 1997 and the decades after, and the question of who the cult leader is drives it to the end. Read the short sequel, 21st Century Boys, straight after; it finishes the story.

Pluto: the shortest way in

Pluto (2003–2009, 8 volumes) retells an Astro Boy story by Osamu Tezuka as a detective thriller. Gesicht, a robot investigator in Europe, is hunting whoever is destroying the seven most advanced robots in the world, of whom he is one. It is about war, grief and whether a machine can hate, and it stands alone even if you have never read Tezuka. Its 2023 anime is a faithful adaptation.

Billy Bat

Billy Bat (2008–2016, 20 volumes), made with his longtime editor Takashi Nagasaki, follows a Japanese-American comic artist who discovers that his cartoon bat has been drawn before, at turning points across history. It is his most ambitious and most divisive series.

The comedies

Before the thrillers, Urasawa's hits were sports comedies for Big Comic Spirits. Yawara! (1986–1993, 29 volumes) follows a girl who is a judo genius and wants only a normal life, while her grandfather plans her Olympic gold. Happy! (1993–1999, 23 volumes) follows a girl who turns professional at tennis to pay off her brother's debt to the yakuza. Both show the same talent for characters, with the tension turned into comedy.

Where to start

For a short, complete thriller, start with Pluto. For his classic, Monster. For a long epic, 20th Century Boys. For comedy, Yawara!. Once you know his rhythm, the rest are easy to find your way into.

faq.question: Do I need to read Astro Boy before Pluto?
faq.answer: No. Pluto retells one Astro Boy story, 'The Greatest Robot on Earth', but it stands entirely on its own. Knowing the original adds to it but is not needed.

faq.question: Is 20th Century Boys finished?
faq.answer: Yes. The main series ran from 1999 to 2006 in 22 volumes, and the story is completed by the short sequel 21st Century Boys, which should be read straight after it.

faq.question: Did Urasawa only write thrillers?
faq.answer: No. His first big hits were sports comedies for Big Comic Spirits: Yawara!, about judo, and Happy!, about tennis. Both are long, light and very funny.

faq.question: Who is Takashi Nagasaki?
faq.answer: Urasawa's longtime editor and collaborator, credited as co-creator on Pluto and Billy Bat. Many of Urasawa's series were developed with him.

title: Where to start with Osamu Tezuka
question: Which Osamu Tezuka manga should I read first?
summary: Start with Black Jack for self-contained stories, Phoenix or Buddha for his epics, or Astro Boy for the classic: a guide to Osamu Tezuka's huge body of work and the best ways into it today. Filed under 7, the inquiry.
body:
7Reduced, this question gives 7. It sits on The Inquiry with the rest of an open question.

Why Tezuka

Osamu Tezuka (1928–1989) is called the god of manga, and the title is not much of an exaggeration. In the decade after the war he brought cinematic pacing, long-form storytelling and expressive, rounded characters to a medium that had mostly meant short gag strips, and almost every manga since inherits something from him. He trained as a doctor, founded an animation studio, and still produced more than 700 titles. Our guide to Tezuka and the invention of modern manga covers his influence; this one is about where to start reading.

Black Jack: the best first read

Black Jack (1973–1983, 25 volumes) ran in Weekly Shōnen Champion. Its hero is an unlicensed surgeon of impossible skill who charges outrageous fees and lives by his own ethics. Each chapter is a complete story: a patient, a moral problem, an operation, and often a twist. Because you can open any volume anywhere, it is the easiest way to see Tezuka at his best, and his medical training shows on every page. It was also his comeback, after a period in the early 1970s when his career seemed to be over.

Phoenix: the life's work

Phoenix (1954–1988) is a cycle of separate stories linked by the phoenix, whose blood grants eternal life. The stories alternate between the distant past and the far future, closing in towards the present, and together they are about birth, death and what people will do to escape them. Tezuka worked on it for most of his career and left it unfinished. Each arc can be read alone; the early-Japan arc called Dawn and the far-future arc called Future are the usual places to begin.

Buddha: the epic

Buddha (1972–1983) retells the life of Siddhartha with a huge invented cast, slapstick, violence and anachronistic jokes. It is reverent about its subject and irreverent about everything else, and its length makes it a commitment, but it is one of the most rewarding long reads in manga.

Astro Boy: the icon

Astro Boy (1952–1968) is a robot boy built by a grieving scientist, who becomes a hero defending humans and robots from each other. It made Tezuka famous and, through its 1963 television series, started Japan's TV anime industry. The early chapters were made for children and can feel dated; many readers come back to it after Black Jack, or through Naoki Urasawa's Pluto, which retells one of its stories for adults.

For adult readers

From the late 1960s, partly in answer to the darker gekiga that young readers were turning to, Tezuka wrote for adults. Message to Adolf follows three men named Adolf through the Second World War. MW is a thriller about a charming killer poisoned by a chemical weapon. Ode to Kirihito is a medical conspiracy about a disease that turns people into dogs. These are the works to read if you think of Tezuka as only a children's artist.

Shōjo and adventure

Princess Knight (1953–1956), about a princess raised as a prince, is one of the founding works of shōjo manga. Dororo (1967–1969), about a young swordsman hunting the demons who stole his body, is a dark samurai fantasy that was recently re-adapted as an anime.

Where to start

Start with Black Jack. Then choose by taste: Phoenix for scope, Buddha for a long epic, Message to Adolf for history, Dororo for action. Read Astro Boy as the historical document it is, and you will see how much came from it.

faq.question: Which Osamu Tezuka manga should I read first?
faq.answer: Black Jack. Its stories are short and self-contained, so you can start anywhere, and they show his range: medical drama, suspense, comedy and moral argument in twenty pages.

faq.question: What is Osamu Tezuka's masterpiece?
faq.answer: Most readers name Phoenix, the cycle of stories he worked on for most of his career, which jumps between the distant past and the far future. Buddha and Black Jack are also often named.

faq.question: How many manga did Osamu Tezuka make?
faq.answer: Over 700 titles and something like 150,000 pages, between his debut in 1946 and his death in 1989, alongside a career running an animation studio.

faq.question: Is Astro Boy a good place to start?
faq.answer: It is his most famous creation, but its early chapters were made for children in the 1950s and can feel dated. Many readers enjoy it more after Black Jack, or through Naoki Urasawa's Pluto, which retells one of its stories for adults.

faq.question: Does Tezuka's manga hold up today?
faq.answer: Yes, with some caveats. His storytelling and ideas are as strong as ever, but some of his caricatures, especially of Black characters, reflect the period; modern editions usually include a note about them.

title: Shōjo fantasy manga
question: What are the best fantasy manga written for girls?
summary: Other worlds, gods, spirits, vampires and magic in shōjo manga, from Princess Knight and The Poe Clan to Fushigi Yūgi, Fruits Basket, Yona of the Dawn and Kamisama Kiss, and where to start reading. The question reduces to 9 — the closing.
body:
9Nine — reckoning. That is the reduction of this question, and the shelf it is read from.

Why shōjo fantasy

Fantasy has been part of shōjo manga since its modern beginnings. Osamu Tezuka's Princess Knight (1953–1956), about a princess raised as a prince, mixed fairy tale and swordplay. Since then, shōjo heroines have travelled to other worlds, served gods, fallen for spirits and vampires, and saved kingdoms. The fantasy is usually a way of telling a story about the heroine: what she wants, what she owes, and who she will become.

The 1970s: The Poe Clan

Moto Hagio's The Poe Clan (1972–1976) follows Edgar and Allan, two boys made vampires and condemned to stay young forever, through two hundred years of European history. It is told in fragments, out of order, from the point of view of the humans who meet them, and it is about loneliness, beauty and time. It is one of the founding works of the Year 24 Group's reinvention of shōjo manga, and every later shōjo vampire story owes it something.

Other worlds

Long before isekai became a genre, shōjo manga sent girls into other worlds. In Yuu Watase's Fushigi Yūgi (1992–1996), Miaka is pulled into an old book set in a version of ancient China, becomes the priestess of a god, and gathers seven celestial warriors, one of whom she falls for. In CLAMP's Magic Knight Rayearth (1993–1996), three schoolgirls are summoned to a magic land to rescue its princess. In Chie Shinohara's Red River, a schoolgirl is pulled into the ancient Hittite empire as a human sacrifice and becomes a political figure. These stories gave their heroines power, loyalty and romance at once, which is the formula modern isekai often borrows.

Gods and spirits

Julietta Suzuki's Kamisama Kiss (2008–2016) makes Nanami, a homeless high-school girl, the god of a small shrine, with a proud fox spirit as her reluctant servant. Yuki Midorikawa's Natsume's Book of Friends follows a boy who can see spirits and returns the names his grandmother took from them. Natsuki Takaya's Fruits Basket (1998–2006) is about the Sōma family, whose members turn into animals of the zodiac, and the girl who comes to live with them; the curse is the frame for a story about abuse and recovery.

Adventure

Mizuho Kusanagi's Yona of the Dawn (2009–) begins on the night a sheltered princess sees her father murdered by the cousin she loved. She flees with her bodyguard and sets out to find the four legendary dragon warriors, growing from a pampered girl into a leader. It is the best modern shōjo adventure, with real politics and war.

Gothic and magic

Matsuri Hino's Vampire Knight (2004–2013) sets a love triangle at an academy where vampire and human students attend separate classes. Arina Tanemura's Phantom Thief Jeanne and Full Moon o Sagashite mix magic with grief and determination; in the second, a girl with a tumour in her throat is given a healthy older body by two death gods so she can sing. The magical-girl stories, from Sailor Moon to Cardcaptor Sakura, are shōjo fantasy too.

Where to start

For adventure, start with Yona of the Dawn. For romance and comedy, Kamisama Kiss. For a 1990s classic, Fushigi Yūgi. For drama, Fruits Basket. For the literary root of it all, The Poe Clan.

faq.question: What is a good shōjo fantasy manga to start with?
faq.answer: Yona of the Dawn is the best modern choice for adventure, Kamisama Kiss for romance and comedy, and Fushigi Yūgi for the 1990s classic. Fruits Basket is the place to start if you want drama with a fantasy twist.

faq.question: Are there shōjo isekai manga?
faq.answer: Yes, and they came long before the genre had a name. Fushigi Yūgi pulls its heroine into a book, Magic Knight Rayearth summons three girls to a magic land, and Red River sends a schoolgirl to the ancient Hittite empire.

faq.question: Is there a shōjo vampire manga?
faq.answer: Vampire Knight, set at an academy where human and vampire students attend separate classes, is the best known. Moto Hagio's The Poe Clan, from the 1970s, is the classic, following two boy vampires through the centuries.

faq.question: Is Fruits Basket a fantasy manga?
faq.answer: Partly. Its premise is supernatural: members of one family turn into animals of the Chinese zodiac when hugged by the opposite sex. But it is mostly a family drama about abuse, trauma and healing.

faq.question: Is Natsume's Book of Friends shōjo?
faq.answer: Yes. It runs in LaLa, a shōjo magazine, though its quiet stories about spirits and loneliness are read by everyone.

title: Where to start with Go Nagai
question: Which Go Nagai manga should I read first?
summary: Start with Devilman for his masterpiece, Mazinger Z for the birth of the piloted giant robot or Cutie Honey for action comedy: a guide to Go Nagai's wild, influential manga and what it gave the medium. Read from the inquiry, as a 7.
body:
7Filed under 7. The Inquiry takes an open question, and this explainer is examines one.

Why Nagai

Go Nagai (born 1945) is one of the most influential manga creators of the 1970s, and one of the most transgressive. A former assistant to Shotaro Ishinomori, he made his name with comedy that shocked parents, then created, within a couple of years, the piloted super robot, the demon-hero and the transforming action heroine. His work is crude, wild and often violent, and much of later manga and anime is built on ideas he had first.

Devilman: the masterpiece

Devilman (1972–1973, 5 volumes) ran in Weekly Shōnen Magazine. Gentle Akira Fudo merges with a demon to fight an invasion of demons, keeping a human heart in a devil's body. The early chapters are monster-of-the-week action; then the story turns on humanity itself, as fear of demons drives people to atrocities worse than anything the demons do. Its ending is one of the most famous and devastating in manga, and its influence runs through decades of dark fantasy, from Berserk to Chainsaw Man. The 2018 anime Devilman Crybaby follows it closely.

Mazinger Z: the robot in the cockpit

Mazinger Z (1972–1974) ran in Weekly Shōnen Jump. A teenager inherits a giant robot built by his grandfather and pilots it against a mad scientist's mechanical beasts. Before Mazinger, giant robots were controlled from outside; Nagai, the story goes, had the idea while stuck in traffic and wishing his car could climb over the cars in front. Putting the hero inside made the robot an extension of him, and that idea is the root of the mecha genre. The manga is brisk and simple; its historical weight is the reason to read it.

Cutie Honey: the transforming heroine

Cutie Honey (1973–1974) ran in Weekly Shōnen Champion. Honey Kisaragi, an android girl, can change her form and costume at will to fight a gang of female villains. It mixes action, comedy and a great deal of fan service, and its transformation sequences fed into the magical-girl genre that followed.

Harenchi Gakuen: the scandal

Harenchi Gakuen (1968–1972), in Weekly Shōnen Jump, was a school comedy about lecherous students and worse teachers. Parents' groups protested and it became a national controversy, which only made it more popular. It is mainly of historical interest now, but it shows how Nagai began by breaking rules, and kept going.

The wider work

With Ken Ishikawa he created Getter Robo, the first combining robot. Violence Jack takes the Devilman world into a post-apocalyptic wasteland. He founded his own company, Dynamic Production, in 1969, which managed his work and its countless adaptations, remakes and crossovers.

Where to start

Start with Devilman, knowing that it is violent and bleak. Read Mazinger Z to see where giant robots come from, and Cutie Honey for the lighter side. If you like what you find, the remakes and spin-offs go on for decades.

faq.question: Which Go Nagai manga should I read first?
faq.answer: Devilman. It is only 5 volumes, it is his most influential work, and its ending is one of the most famous in manga. Be aware that it is extremely violent.

faq.question: Did Go Nagai invent giant robots?
faq.answer: No, but he invented the piloted one. Before Mazinger Z in 1972, giant robots were controlled remotely; Nagai put the hero inside, in a cockpit, and that idea underlies Gundam, Evangelion and almost every mecha since.

faq.question: Is the Devilman manga the same as Devilman Crybaby?
faq.answer: Devilman Crybaby, the 2018 anime directed by Masaaki Yuasa, follows the manga's story and ending closely but moves it to the present day. The original 1972 anime was a different, child-friendly story made alongside the manga.

faq.question: Why was Go Nagai controversial?
faq.answer: His first hit, Harenchi Gakuen, was a school comedy with nudity and slapstick that provoked protests from parents' groups. Nagai kept testing the limits of what shōnen manga could show, in sex and violence alike, and later artists benefited from the space he opened.

faq.question: Who did Go Nagai work for before his debut?
faq.answer: He was an assistant to Shotaro Ishinomori, the creator of Cyborg 009, before making his own debut in 1967.

title: Shōjo manga of the 1990s
question: What were the great shōjo manga of the 1990s?
summary: Sailor Moon, Boys Over Flowers, Marmalade Boy, Fushigi Yūgi and Fruits Basket: the decade when shōjo magazines sold in millions, their heroines became anime stars, and shōjo manga found its first large audience abroad. Read from the turn, as a 5.
body:
5A 5 by its question: freedom seeker, and therefore the turn.

A golden decade

The 1990s were the commercial peak of shōjo manga. The big monthly magazines for girls sold in numbers that now seem impossible: Ribon sold around 2.3 million copies an issue at its 1994 peak, and Nakayoshi, carried by Sailor Moon, was not far behind. A hit in one of these magazines became an anime almost automatically, and the anime carried it abroad. The stories that defined the decade fall into a few families: magical girls who fight, romances with complicated families, and girls pulled into fantasy worlds.

Magical girls who fight

Naoko Takeuchi's Sailor Moon (1991–1997), in Nakayoshi, changed the magical girl. Usagi is a clumsy schoolgirl who becomes the leader of a team of soldiers, each with her own planet, power and personality, fighting a succession of villains in a story that grows into a cosmic romance. The team structure owed something to boys' hero shows, and the result appealed to everyone. Nakayoshi followed it with CLAMP's Magic Knight Rayearth (1993–1996) and Cardcaptor Sakura (1996–2000); Ribon answered with Arina Tanemura's Phantom Thief Jeanne (1998–2000), whose heroine is a reincarnation of Joan of Arc stealing paintings possessed by demons.

Romance and family

Yōko Kamio's Boys Over Flowers (1992–2003, 37 volumes), in Margaret, follows Tsukushi, a working-class girl at an elite school who stands up to the four rich boys who rule it, and falls for their leader. It is a Cinderella story with a heroine who refuses to be rescued, and it became one of the best-selling shōjo manga ever, remade as television drama in Taiwan, Japan and Korea. In Ribon, Wataru Yoshizumi's Marmalade Boy (1992–1995) begins when a girl's parents announce they are swapping partners with another couple, leaving her sharing a house with their son. Ai Yazawa's Gokinjo Monogatari (1995–1998) brought fashion and creative ambition into Ribon, and Miho Obana's Kodocha mixed child-star comedy with real family pain. Together they pushed the magazine towards older, more stylish heroines.

Other worlds

Long before isekai was a genre, shōjo heroines were falling into other worlds. Yuu Watase's Fushigi Yūgi (1992–1996), in Shōjo Comic, pulls Miaka into a book set in a version of ancient China, where she becomes the priestess of a god and is protected by seven celestial warriors. Watase followed it with Ceres, Celestial Legend (1996–2000), a darker story about a girl who carries the spirit of a vengeful celestial maiden. Chie Shinohara's Red River sent its heroine to the Hittite empire. Natsuki Takaya's Fruits Basket, begun in Hana to Yume in 1998, set a zodiac curse inside a family drama and became one of the defining shōjo manga of the next decade. Our guide to shōjo fantasy manga follows this line further.

Going global

Sailor Moon's anime reached North American television in 1995, and its manga followed in English a few years later. For many readers outside Japan, it was the first manga they knew was manga. Through the late 1990s and the 2000s, publishers translated the decade's hits in quick succession, and they found a readership that had barely been served before: girls and young women. That audience changed the English-language manga market, and much of it was built on the 1990s.

The background

The decade stood on the work of the 1970s, when the Year 24 Group and series like The Rose of Versailles showed what shōjo manga could do with history, psychology and romance. The 1990s took that ambition and made it popular on a vast scale.

Where to start

Begin with Sailor Moon, the series that defines the decade. For romance, try Marmalade Boy, which is short, or Boys Over Flowers, which is not. For fantasy, Fushigi Yūgi. For magic with a gentler touch, Cardcaptor Sakura.

faq.question: What was the most popular shōjo manga of the 1990s?
faq.answer: Sailor Moon was the decade's global phenomenon, through its anime as much as the manga. Boys Over Flowers, which began in 1992, went on to become one of the best-selling shōjo manga of all time.

faq.question: Why were the 1990s so important for shōjo manga?
faq.answer: The big shōjo magazines reached record circulations, their hits were adapted into anime almost as a matter of course, and those anime carried shōjo stories abroad. The first large English-speaking readership for shōjo manga grew out of that decade.

faq.question: Which 1990s shōjo manga were made into anime?
faq.answer: Most of the big ones: Sailor Moon, Marmalade Boy, Fushigi Yūgi, Magic Knight Rayearth, Cardcaptor Sakura, Gokinjo Monogatari, Phantom Thief Jeanne and Boys Over Flowers all have anime adaptations, and Boys Over Flowers was also remade as live-action drama in Taiwan, Japan and Korea.

faq.question: Is Fruits Basket a 1990s manga?
faq.answer: It began in 1998 and ran until 2006, so it belongs to both decades. It is often grouped with the late-1990s wave because it started then, but most of it was published in the 2000s.

faq.question: Which 1990s shōjo manga should I read first?
faq.answer: Sailor Moon is the one that defines the decade. For romance, Marmalade Boy is short at 8 volumes; for fantasy, Fushigi Yūgi; for something long and addictive, Boys Over Flowers.

title: Where to start with Ai Yazawa
question: Which Ai Yazawa manga should I read first?
summary: Start with Paradise Kiss for a complete story in 5 volumes, Nana for her masterpiece or Gokinjo Monogatari for her shōjo roots: a guide to Ai Yazawa's fashion-filled stories about young women finding their way. 112 in the letters, reducing to 4.
body:
4The letters of this question total 112, a 4 — the number of structure, labour, and the building of lasting systems.

Why Yazawa

Ai Yazawa (born 1967) is the manga creator of fashion, friendship and young women deciding who to become. She studied fashion design before turning to manga, and her pages are full of clothes drawn with real knowledge: punk, couture, school uniforms worn wrong on purpose. Her stories are about ambitious, flawed, funny women, and they are honest about love in a way that made her one of the defining voices of 1990s and 2000s shōjo and josei manga.

Nana: the masterpiece

Nana (2000–, 21 volumes) ran in Cookie. Two twenty-year-old women named Nana meet on a train to Tokyo and end up sharing an apartment. Nana Osaki is a punk singer chasing a record deal; Nana Komatsu, nicknamed Hachi, falls in love easily and wants someone to look after. The series follows them, their bands and their boyfriends through success, heartbreak and bad decisions, and it is above all a story about a friendship between two very different women. It won the Shogakukan Manga Award, sold tens of millions of copies and was adapted into two films and an anime. It has been on hiatus since 2009, when Yazawa fell ill.

Paradise Kiss: the complete one

Paradise Kiss (1999–2003, 5 volumes) ran in Zipper, a fashion magazine. Yukari, a studious high-school girl, is scouted by fashion-school students who need a model for their graduation show, and is pulled into their world and into a romance with George, their charming and difficult designer. It is short, stylish and ends with real courage. If you want to know whether Yazawa is for you, start here.

Gokinjo Monogatari: the roots

Gokinjo Monogatari (1995–1998, 7 volumes) ran in Ribon, a magazine for young girls. Mikako, a student at an art and fashion school who dreams of her own brand, falls for her childhood friend who lives next door. It is lighter and younger than her later work, but it is where her interest in fashion and creative ambition takes shape, and Paradise Kiss picks up threads from its world.

The earlier work

Yazawa made her debut in Ribon in the 1980s, and her first big hit there was Tenshi Nanka Ja Nai, a school romance. Her work in Ribon helped push the magazine towards older, more stylish heroines through the 1990s; our guide to shōjo manga of the 1990s has the context.

The style

Yazawa draws long-limbed, fashionable figures and pays close attention to how her characters dress and decorate their rooms. Her narration is often in a character's own voice, looking back, which gives even happy scenes a note of what came after.

Where to start

Start with Paradise Kiss for a complete story. Read Nana next, accepting that it has no ending yet. Go back to Gokinjo Monogatari to see where it all began.

faq.question: Which Ai Yazawa manga should I read first?
faq.answer: Paradise Kiss: it is complete in 5 volumes and shows her fashion, humour and emotional honesty at their best. Nana is her masterpiece but has no ending.

faq.question: Will Nana ever be finished?
faq.answer: Nobody knows. Nana has been on hiatus since 2009, when Yazawa fell ill, after 21 volumes. She has since done illustration work and has said she still hopes to finish it, but no new chapters of Nana have appeared.

faq.question: Is Nana still worth reading without an ending?
faq.answer: Most readers say yes. The 21 volumes contain a great deal of story, and flash-forwards in the series show where several characters end up, so it feels less unresolved than its hiatus suggests.

faq.question: Are Paradise Kiss and Gokinjo Monogatari connected?
faq.answer: Yes. Paradise Kiss is set in the same world and features characters connected to Gokinjo Monogatari, including the younger sister of its heroine. Each can be read alone.

faq.question: Is Ai Yazawa shojo or josei?
faq.answer: Both. She began in the shōjo magazine Ribon, and her best-known later works, Paradise Kiss and Nana, ran in magazines for older readers and are usually classed as josei.

title: Delinquent manga: from Joe to Tokyo Revengers
question: What are the best delinquent manga?
summary: Manga about delinquents, school gangs and motorcycle crews, from Ashita no Joe and Crows to Great Teacher Onizuka and Tokyo Revengers: what the genre is built on and where to start reading it. The question reduces to 5 — the turn.
body:
5Filed under 5. The Turn takes a turn, and this explainer is changes one.

What delinquent manga are

Delinquent manga, called yankī manga in Japan, are about young people who reject the rules: high-school fighters, motorcycle gangs and outsiders. The style is instantly recognisable: pompadours, long embroidered coats, school uniforms worn open, and a strict code of honour that has nothing to do with the school's. The stories are built on fights, but what they are about is loyalty, rivalry, respect earned by standing your ground, and finding a group that will have you.

The roots: Ashita no Joe

Ikki Kajiwara and Tetsuya Chiba's Ashita no Joe (1968–1973), in Weekly Shōnen Magazine, follows Joe Yabuki, a drifter from the Tokyo slums who learns to box in juvenile detention and fights his way up, burning himself out completely. Its rebel hero, loyal to nobody but his rivals, became a model for decades of delinquent stories, and its last image is one of the most famous in manga.

The 1980s and the gang boom

Delinquency was a real social concern in 1980s Japan, with motorcycle gangs, known as bōsōzoku, and violence in schools, and manga turned it into entertainment. Kazuhiro Kiuchi's Be-Bop High School, in Young Magazine, made the school fighter a comic hero. Masanori Morita's Rokudenashi Blues, in Weekly Shōnen Jump, followed a delinquent boxer at a Tokyo high school. Tōru Fujisawa's Shonan Junai Gumi followed two gang members trying, and failing, to find girlfriends.

Crows: the school-gang classic

Hiroshi Takahashi's Crows (1990–1998, 26 volumes), in Monthly Shōnen Champion, is set at Suzuran, a boys' school so violent that no one has ever ruled it. Harumichi Bōya, a transfer student who fights for fun and has no interest in leading, becomes its legend. There are almost no girls and no classes, only factions, alliances and fights, and it is the reference point for the genre. It continued in Worst and inspired the Crows Zero films.

Great Teacher Onizuka

Fujisawa's Great Teacher Onizuka (1997–2002) takes Onizuka, one of the gang members from Shonan Junai Gumi, and makes him a 22-year-old teacher. He is crude, broke and unqualified, and he takes on the worst class in his school by caring more about its students than anyone else does. It is one of the best-loved manga of its decade, and it shows the genre's heart: the delinquent as the one adult who will not give up on you.

The modern revival

Ken Wakui's Tokyo Revengers (2017–2022, 31 volumes) brought the genre back to a new generation by adding time travel. Takemichi, a 26-year-old with nothing going for him, learns that his middle-school girlfriend has been killed in a gang conflict, and finds himself sent back twelve years to the delinquent days he wasted. To save her, he has to change the history of the Tokyo Manji Gang from inside. Its anime and live-action films made it a hit far beyond Japan.

Comedy and variations

Ryūhei Tamura's Beelzebub (2009–2014) gives the strongest delinquent at the worst school in Japan the baby son of the demon king to raise. Oh! great's Air Gear turns gang wars into battles on motorised roller skates. The genre's codes are so familiar that they work in almost any setting.

Where to start

For the classic, start with Crows. For heart, Great Teacher Onizuka. For something modern, Tokyo Revengers. For comedy, Beelzebub. For the ancestor of all of them, Ashita no Joe.

faq.question: What is a delinquent manga?
faq.answer: A manga about rebellious young people, usually high-school fighters or motorcycle gang members, built on fights, loyalty, rivalry and the search for a place to belong. In Japan they are called yankī manga, after the slang for a delinquent.

faq.question: What is the classic delinquent manga?
faq.answer: Crows, set at a boys' school no one has ever ruled, is the reference point for the school-gang story. Ashita no Joe, from 1968, is the older ancestor of the rebel hero.

faq.question: Is Great Teacher Onizuka a delinquent manga?
faq.answer: Yes, in its own way. Its hero is a former gang member who becomes a teacher, and he first appeared in Tōru Fujisawa's earlier delinquent series, Shonan Junai Gumi.

faq.question: What is Tokyo Revengers about?
faq.answer: A man in his twenties travels back to his delinquent school days to save his ex-girlfriend from being killed, and has to change the history of a Tokyo motorcycle gang to do it. It ran from 2017 to 2022 in 31 volumes.

faq.question: Are there funny delinquent manga?
faq.answer: Yes. Beelzebub has a school's toughest fighter raising the son of the demon king, and many classic delinquent series are as much comedy as action.

title: Monster partners in manga
question: What are some manga where the hero is partnered with a monster or spirit?
summary: Heroes and their monstrous companions, from Ushio and Tora, Parasyte and Devilman to Natsume's Nyanko-sensei, Shaman King's ghost samurai and Chainsaw Man's Pochita: why the human-and-monster partnership works and where to start. Read from the structure, as a 4.
body:
4A 4 by its question: builder & organizer, and therefore the structure.

The odd couple

A great many manga pair a human hero with a monster: a spirit, a demon, an alien or a yōkai. The pattern is old, with roots in folk tales about people who strike bargains with spirits, and it suits serialised storytelling perfectly. The monster brings power the hero lacks; the hero brings a conscience the monster lacks; and the relationship between them, usually beginning in mistrust, gives the story an emotional line that can run for years.

Reluctant allies

Kazuhiro Fujita's Ushio and Tora (1990–1996, 33 volumes) is the classic. Ushio, a temple priest's son, finds a monster pinned to the cellar wall by a spear for five hundred years, and frees it. Tora swears to eat him at the first chance, and spends the series fighting at his side instead. Hitoshi Iwaaki's Parasyte (1988–1995) is the horror version: an alien parasite, meant to take over Shinichi's brain, ends up in his right hand. Migi is cold, curious and entirely logical, and their partnership is a long argument about what being human is worth.

Spirit guardians

Yuki Midorikawa's Natsume's Book of Friends (2003–) is the gentle version. Natsume, a lonely boy who can see spirits, inherits his grandmother's book of their names, and the powerful spirit Madara agrees to guard him, in the shape of a fat lucky cat, on condition that he gets the book when Natsume dies. Hiroyuki Takei's Shaman King (1998–2004) gives every fighter a partner spirit; Yoh's is the ghost of a samurai six hundred years dead. Shigeru Mizuki's GeGeGe no Kitarō, the grandfather of yōkai manga, gives its hero his dead father's eyeball as a constant companion.

Fighting spirits

Hirohiko Araki's JoJo's Bizarre Adventure turned the partner into a power system. From its third part onwards, fighters have Stands, spirits that embody their will and fight for them, each with its own strange ability. ONE's Mob Psycho 100 has Dimple, a scheming evil spirit who attaches himself to the psychic hero, hoping to use him, and becomes his friend.

Merged

Some heroes do not partner with a monster so much as become one. In Go Nagai's Devilman (1972–1973), Akira merges with a demon to fight the demons, keeping a human heart in a devil's body; it set the model for dark fantasy. In Tatsuki Fujimoto's Chainsaw Man (2018–2026), Denji's devil dog Pochita becomes his heart, literally. In Yūsei Matsui's Neuro, the arrangement is reversed: the demon who eats mysteries is the detective, and the human girl is his unwilling public face.

At home

The monster can also come home. In coolkyousinnjya's Miss Kobayashi's Dragon Maid, a dragon whose life a programmer saved moves in as her maid, and the comedy of a vast and ancient being doing housework becomes a story about a found family.

Why it works

The partnership gives the hero power without making him the most powerful person in the story, and it gives the writer a second point of view: someone who sees humans from outside. The best of these stories are about the monster learning to care, and the human learning that caring is not a weakness.

Where to start

For the classic, start with Ushio and Tora. For horror, Parasyte. For gentleness, Natsume's Book of Friends. For action, Shaman King. For the darkest version, Devilman.

faq.question: What is a good manga about a boy and a monster?
faq.answer: Ushio and Tora, about a temple boy and the monster he frees, is the classic: the monster swears to eat the boy, and they fight side by side for 33 volumes.

faq.question: Is Parasyte a monster-partner manga?
faq.answer: Yes. An alien parasite fails to take over a boy's brain and settles in his right hand instead, and the two must work together to survive the other parasites.

faq.question: Are there gentle monster-partner stories?
faq.answer: Natsume's Book of Friends pairs a lonely boy with a powerful spirit who usually looks like a fat cat. Miss Kobayashi's Dragon Maid is a comedy about a dragon who becomes an office worker's maid.

faq.question: Why are monster-partner stories so popular?
faq.answer: They combine power with friendship. The partnership usually starts with mistrust or open threats, and the monster's slow, grudging loyalty is often the most moving thing in the story.

faq.question: Is Devilman a monster-partner manga?
faq.answer: In the most extreme form: its hero merges with a demon, keeping a human heart in a devil's body. It is the model for the many later stories in which hero and monster share one body.

title: Where to start with Hiromu Arakawa
question: Which Hiromu Arakawa manga should I read first?
summary: Start with Fullmetal Alchemist for her masterpiece, Silver Spoon for something gentler or The Heroic Legend of Arslan for epic fantasy: a guide to Hiromu Arakawa's manga and the farm-bred practicality that runs through them. The question reduces to 3 — the telling.
body:
3Three — expression. That is the reduction of this question, and the shelf it is read from.

Why Arakawa

Hiromu Arakawa (born 1973) grew up on a dairy farm in Hokkaido and worked on it for years before becoming a manga artist. That background runs through the work: a practical, unsentimental sense of how much effort things cost, how bodies work, and how food reaches the table. Arakawa's stories are tightly plotted, funny in the middle of disaster, and generous to every character, villains included.

Fullmetal Alchemist: the masterpiece

Fullmetal Alchemist (2001–2010, 27 volumes) ran in Monthly Shōnen Gangan. Two brothers, Edward and Alphonse Elric, try to bring their dead mother back with alchemy; the attempt costs Ed an arm and a leg and Al his whole body, leaving his soul bound to a suit of armour. Their search for a way to restore themselves leads into a military conspiracy that reaches the top of their country. The magic system rests on one rule, equivalent exchange, and the story keeps testing it. It is a battle shōnen with the plotting of a thriller, it deals seriously with war and genocide, and it ends exactly where it meant to. It is one of the most widely recommended manga of all time.

Silver Spoon: the gentle one

Silver Spoon (2011–2019, 15 volumes) ran in Weekly Shōnen Sunday. Yugo Hachiken, burnt out by exam pressure, enrols at an agricultural high school in rural Hokkaido because it has dormitories far from home. He knows nothing about farming and is surrounded by students who will inherit farms. The series is about work, animals, food and the economics of agriculture, and about a boy who has never been allowed to choose anything learning what he wants. It won the Manga Taishō, and it is the best choice if you want Arakawa without the battles.

The Heroic Legend of Arslan: the epic

The Heroic Legend of Arslan (2013–) runs in Bessatsu Shōnen Magazine and adapts Yoshiki Tanaka's fantasy novels. Arslan, the gentle crown prince of a kingdom inspired by ancient Persia, survives the destruction of his father's army and gathers a band of followers to win the kingdom back. It is an epic of war and statecraft, and Arakawa's battlefield staging is superb.

The essay manga

Noble Farmer (Hyakushō Kizoku), an essay manga about Arakawa's years on the farm, is full of absurd stories about cows, weather and Hokkaido winters. It is the clearest view of where the practical streak in the fiction comes from, and where the cow self-portrait does too.

The newer work

Daemons of the Shadow Realm, which began in 2021 in Monthly Shōnen Gangan, the magazine that ran Fullmetal Alchemist, is a fantasy about twins in a mountain village and the guardian spirits bound to them.

Where to start

Start with Fullmetal Alchemist. If you want something gentler afterwards, read Silver Spoon; if you want more war and politics, Arslan.

faq.answer: Fullmetal Alchemist. It is complete in 27 volumes, tightly plotted from start to finish, and one of the most widely recommended manga of all time.

faq.answer: The manga is the original and complete story. Of the two anime, Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood (2009) follows it closely; the 2003 series departs from it to tell its own ending.

faq.answer: A city boy who enrols at an agricultural high school in Hokkaido to escape academic pressure, and learns about farm work, animals and food. It draws on Arakawa's own upbringing on a dairy farm and won the Manga Taishō.

title: Japanese Honorifics in Manga: -san, -kun, -chan, -sama and More
question: What do -san, -kun, -chan and -sama mean in manga?
summary: Japanese adds a suffix to most names to show how the speaker relates to the person: -san is polite, -kun is for boys and juniors, -chan is affectionate, -sama is deferential, and leaving the suffix off altogether signals either closeness or rudeness. Read from the care, as a 6.
body:
6A 6 by its question: nurturer & harmonizer, and therefore the care.

The short version

In Japanese, a name almost never appears on its own. It carries a suffix, and the suffix tells you how the speaker sees the person: as a stranger, a friend, a junior, a superior or someone to be adored. Manga uses these suffixes the way an English novel uses tone of voice, and a change of suffix can carry as much weight as a confession.

-san: the default

-san is the neutral polite suffix, used for adults, classmates you do not know well, colleagues, neighbours and strangers, regardless of gender. It is the safe choice, roughly the territory of Mr or Ms but used with first names as well as surnames. It even attaches to shops and trades: a bookseller can be called hon'ya-san.

-kun: boys, juniors and subordinates

-kun is used mostly for boys and young men, by people of the same age or older. Teachers use it for male students; in offices a manager may use it for junior staff of either gender. In Detective Conan, Ran calls the shrunken detective Conan-kun, the right suffix for a small boy she has taken in, and the joke is that he is really the high-school boyfriend she would address quite differently.

-chan: affection

-chan is a diminutive. It is used for small children, close friends (especially between girls), grandparents, pets and anyone the speaker finds cute. Used on an adult man, it is either a mark of long intimacy or a tease; used on oneself, it reads as childish. The even more babyish -tan appears in comedy and in fan culture.

-sama: deference

-sama is the deferential form: for customers, for nobility, for gods and for people a character worships. Retainers in historical manga address their lords this way, and a romantic lead can be called -sama by an admirer. When an arrogant character refers to himself as ore-sama, he is awarding himself the honorific, which is the joke. The title of Kaguya-sama: Love Is War uses it to tell you, before the first page, how the school sees its heroine.

-dono and other period forms

-dono is an older respectful form found in samurai-era settings and formal documents. In Rurouni Kenshin, the wandering swordsman calls Kaoru Kaoru-dono, an old-fashioned courtesy that marks him as a man out of his time and as someone deliberately humble. Historical manga use such forms the way a costume drama uses period speech.

Titles that work like suffixes

Some words act as honorifics on their own or after a name. Senpai is anyone senior to you in a school, club or workplace, and kohai is the junior. Sensei is for teachers, doctors, lawyers and masters of a craft, including manga artists, which is why fans write of Oda-sensei. Family words such as onii-san (big brother) and onee-san (big sister) are also used for young people who are not related to the speaker at all.

No suffix at all

Calling someone by name with nothing attached is called yobisute. Between family members, close friends and couples it is natural. Anywhere else it is blunt, and a character who does it to a stranger is being rude, overfamiliar or both. Romance manga build scenes around the first time a couple drop the suffix; delinquent manga use bare surnames to show who is in charge.

How to read the shifts

Because honorifics are chosen, they change. A classmate who goes from a surname with -san to a first name with -kun has become a friend. A character who suddenly adds -san to someone they used to call by name is creating distance, usually after a fight. In a tsundere romance, the moment the prickly lead slips and uses an affectionate form is often the payoff of several volumes.

Why translations differ

English has no system that does this work, so translators choose. Some keep the suffixes and print a short explanation; others translate them into first names, surnames, nicknames and tone of voice. Anime subtitles have the same problem, and the dub of a series may make a different choice from its print edition. Neither approach is wrong, but knowing what the suffixes mean lets you notice what a translation has had to leave out. Our guide to lettering and translation choices covers the wider problem.

faq.question: What is the difference between -kun and -chan?
faq.answer: -kun is most often used for boys and for juniors, and by a superior to a subordinate of either gender in a workplace. -chan is a diminutive used for small children, close friends, girls and anyone the speaker finds cute. Calling a grown man -chan is either very intimate or a deliberate tease.

faq.question: What does it mean when a character drops the honorific?
faq.answer: Using a name with no suffix at all, called yobisute, signals either real intimacy, as between family, old friends and couples, or a lack of respect. Manga often marks a turning point in a relationship by having one character drop the suffix for the first time.

faq.question: Why do some translations keep honorifics and others drop them?
faq.answer: Neither choice is complete. Keeping them preserves information but asks the reader to learn a small piece of Japanese; dropping them reads more naturally but loses the shifts in relationship they encode. Publishers often decide series by series, and fan readers tend to prefer them kept.

faq.question: Is senpai an honorific?
faq.answer: Yes. Senpai, kohai and sensei are titles that can be used on their own or after a name, and they work like the suffixes: they place the two speakers in a relationship of seniority or expertise.

faq.question: What does -sama mean in a manga title?
faq.answer: -sama is the most deferential everyday suffix, used for customers, nobility, gods and people the speaker serves or idolises. In Kaguya-sama: Love Is War it marks the heroine as the daughter of a powerful family whom everyone at school treats with awe.

title: Manga, Manhwa and Manhua: What's the Difference?
question: What is the difference between manga, manhwa and manhua?
summary: Manga is Japanese, manhwa is Korean and manhua is Chinese: the three words are the same term in three languages, and the real differences are in reading direction, colour, format and the platforms each grew up on. The question reduces to 1 — the opening.
body:
1Filed under 1. The Opening takes a first move, and this explainer is declares one.

The same word in three languages

Manga, manhwa and manhua are the Japanese, Korean and Chinese readings of the same two characters, meaning something like "whimsical pictures". In English each has come to mean the comics of its own country: manga from Japan, manhwa from Korea, manhua from mainland China, Hong Kong and Taiwan. The words tell you where a comic was made, not what it looks like, but in practice the three now arrive in quite different shapes.

Reading direction

Japanese manga reads right to left, because Japanese books open from what an English reader thinks of as the back. Printed Korean manhwa reads left to right, like English. Printed manhua has varied by place and period, but English editions almost all read left to right. Most new manhwa and manhua avoid the question altogether, because they are made to scroll down a phone screen.

Format: the book and the scroll

Manga is still built around the printed page. Chapters run in weekly or monthly magazines and are collected into volumes, and even manga published first on apps is usually drawn as pages that can be printed. Since the 2000s most new manhwa has been drawn as a webtoon: a single long vertical strip per episode, read by scrolling. Naver Webtoon, launched in Korea in 2004, made the format mainstream; Tower of God, serialised there from 2010, was one of the first to find a large audience abroad. Chinese platforms adopted the same format for most new manhua. The scroll changes how a story is told. A page reveals a whole layout at once, while a scroll controls exactly when each image appears, so the empty space between panels does the work that a page turn does in manga. Our guide to how webtoons differ from manga goes into the craft.

Colour

Manga is mostly black and white, with screentone and hatching doing the work of colour, because it grew up in cheap weekly magazines where colour pages were costly and rare. Webtoon manhwa and manhua are almost always in full colour, often with heavy digital painting, because the screen makes colour free to the reader.

Studios and solo artists

A Japanese manga is usually credited to one mangaka, or a writer and an artist, with assistants behind them. Webtoons, with an episode every week in full colour, are often made by studios that divide the work into line art, colour, backgrounds and lettering. Solo Leveling, adapted from a Korean web novel, was drawn by the artist known as Dubu with Redice Studio, and its success helped make the studio model standard.

Genres each is known for

All three cover everything, but each has strengths that readers recognise. Manga has the deepest catalogue of long-running battle shonen, sports and slice-of-life series. Manhwa is especially known for leveling fantasy, regression and revenge stories, and romance fantasy, many of them adapted from web novels. Manhua has a long tradition of martial-arts stories: Hong Kong comics such as Tony Wong's Oriental Heroes, which began in 1970, and Ma Wing-shing's Storm Riders made martial arts the backbone of Hong Kong comics, and modern manhua continues that line with cultivation fantasy in which heroes grow in power through training.

Why they get confused

In English the three are sold on the same shelves and apps, adapted into anime by the same studios and discussed in the same forums, so "manga" is often used for all of them. That is understandable but not accurate, and the differences are not trivial: a black-and-white page read from right to left and a colour strip scrolled downwards are different ways of telling a story.

Where to start

If you know manga and want to try manhwa, Tower of God shows what the scroll format can do with a long fantasy, and Solo Leveling shows why leveling stories became so popular. If you are coming the other way, from webtoons to manga, start with something short and in clean grids, such as those in our list of twelve manga to start with.

The 1 mistakes being first for being right. Several of these texts describe launches that mattered enormously for a year and then mattered to nobody. What the 1 still asks is that you notice what had to not exist for this to be possible. The other explainers that reduce to 1 are collected on The Opening.

faq.question: Is manhwa the same as manga?
faq.answer: No. Manhwa is the Korean word for comics and covers comics made in Korea. It shares a root with the word manga, but it has its own history, and modern manhwa is usually published as a full-colour vertical-scroll webtoon rather than as a black-and-white book.

faq.question: Which way do you read manhwa and manhua?
faq.answer: Webtoon-format manhwa and manhua scroll from top to bottom, so direction is not an issue. Printed Korean manhwa reads left to right like English. Printed manhua from Hong Kong and Taiwan has varied, but most modern editions in English read left to right. Only Japanese manga keeps the right-to-left order.

faq.question: Is Solo Leveling a manga?
faq.answer: No. Solo Leveling is a Korean manhwa, adapted from a Korean web novel and serialised as a webtoon. It is often called a manga in English because it reached many readers through the same shops, apps and anime fandom.

faq.question: Why are manhwa and manhua in colour?
faq.answer: Most were made for phones. Vertical-scroll comics are published one episode at a time on platforms where colour costs the reader nothing extra, while Japanese manga grew up in cheap black-and-white magazines where colour pages were expensive.

title: The Dere Types Explained: Tsundere, Yandere, Kuudere and Dandere
question: What are tsundere, yandere, kuudere and dandere?
summary: The dere types are fan labels for how a character shows affection: a tsundere hides it behind hostility, a yandere's turns dangerous, a kuudere's stays under a calm surface, and a dandere's is held back by shyness. The question reduces to 6 — the care.
body:
6Six — responsibility. That is the reduction of this question, and the shelf it is read from.

Where the word comes from

Deredere is a Japanese mimetic word for being lovestruck, all soft and affectionate. Fans began attaching it to other words to describe how a character's affection shows up, or fails to. The first and most durable was tsundere, from tsuntsun, prickly and aloof. The label spread through Japanese fan culture around the turn of the 2000s, from romance games into anime and manga discussion, and a family of similar coinages followed. None of them are formal categories, but they are a quick way to say how a character loves.

Tsundere: hostile on the outside

A tsundere treats the person they care about with irritation, insults or violence, while the reader can see the feeling underneath. The appeal is the gap between the two, and the slow moments when the warmth breaks through. Asuka Langley Soryu in Neon Genesis Evangelion is the reference point most fans reach for; Akane Tendo in Rumiko Takahashi's Ranma ½ shows the pattern was in place long before it had a name. A tsundere's arc is usually about learning to say what they feel.

Yandere: love that becomes dangerous

A yandere, from yanderu, to be sick, begins as sweet and devoted, and the devotion turns obsessive and violent. They will hurt rivals, or the beloved, to keep them. Yuno Gasai of Future Diary is the character most often cited. The type works in horror and thrillers because it takes a romantic ideal, total devotion, and follows it to its logical end.

Kuudere: calm on the surface

A kuudere, from the English word cool, is composed, flat-voiced and hard to read. They care, but show it in small acts rather than words. Rei Ayanami, also from Evangelion, is the classic example, which is one reason that series is so often used to explain these terms: its two leading girls are opposite types. The pleasure of a kuudere is watching for the rare moment their expression changes.

Dandere: quiet from shyness

A dandere is quiet because talking is hard, not because they feel little. They open up only with people they trust, and the story is often the process of earning that trust. Hinata Hyuga in Naruto is a well-known example, and Shoko Komi in Komi Can't Communicate builds a whole series around a heroine whose silence everyone misreads as coolness.

Other types fans use

The list keeps growing. Deredere on its own describes a character who is openly cheerful and affectionate with no gap to resolve. Himedere wants to be treated like a princess; kamidere believes they are a god; bakadere is lovably clumsy. These are mostly jokes built on the same pattern, and few readers use them with a straight face.

Why the labels are useful, and where they stop

The dere types describe a gap between how a character behaves and what they feel, and that gap is what drives a lot of romantic comedy. Naming it helps readers find stories they will like and see how a scene is built. But the labels are fan shorthand, not something creators set out to fill in, and the best characters slip between them. Kaguya Shinomiya of Kaguya-sama: Love Is War behaves like a tsundere and thinks like a strategist, and the series gets its comedy from the fact that neither lead will be the first to admit anything. If you are new to fan vocabulary in general, our guide to manga fandom vocabulary covers the rest.

faq.question: What does dere mean?
faq.answer: Dere comes from deredere, a Japanese mimetic word for being lovestruck or sweetly affectionate. Every dere type joins it to a second word that describes how a character behaves before the affection shows: tsuntsun for prickly, yanderu for sick, kuuru for cool.

faq.question: Who is the most famous tsundere?
faq.answer: Asuka Langley Soryu of Neon Genesis Evangelion is the usual reference point, and Akane Tendo of Ranma ½ is an older example of the same pattern. The label itself spread in the early 2000s, so many earlier characters were described as tsundere only in hindsight.

faq.question: What is the difference between kuudere and dandere?
faq.answer: Both are quiet, but for different reasons. A kuudere is composed and seems unmoved; a dandere is shy and finds talking difficult. A kuudere is calm and in control, while a dandere is anxious and would talk more if they could.

faq.question: Are the dere types official categories?
faq.answer: No. They are fan vocabulary, not terms that publishers or creators use to design characters. They are useful shorthand for how affection is shown, but most good characters fit them only partly, and the most interesting ones change type as the story goes on.
